articles.title_orig: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
articles.title_zh: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG (AP) — With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.
As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the two AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the U.S.-led Pax Silica and the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization.
That could put many countries in a dilemma: Do they go with the U.S.’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?
Kazakhstan, a Central Asia nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.
Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the U.S. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China's initiative to shape the global AI agenda.
Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.
“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.
“We don’t want this binary choice,” Masalimova said.
Kazakhstan is benefiting from both U.S. and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” she said,
It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the U.S.
Earlier this year, Kazakhstan's government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.
Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.
Both China and the U.S. are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.
President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” U.S. officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.
Beijing has rejected those claims and says the U.S. is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.
Washington has signaled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.
“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the U.S. State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.
For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World AI Cooperation Organization. “As both major countries in AI, China and the United States should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement. “AI should not be owned by major countries.”
The two AI powers have different messaging largely because Beijing needs to court third countries in its bid to build an alternative coalition, whereas Washington already has a powerful network of allies, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.
That lends power to what he described as “swing countries.”
Like Kazakhstan, Indonesia has resources vital for AI and other technologies, such as nickel and copper. It's also seeking to make the most of both AI powers, having joined China's World AI Cooperation Organization.
Indonesia wants to benefit from both, Mari Pangestu, Indonesian National Economic Council's vice chair, told reporters at a University of Hong Kong Business School event. “We should be able to be part of both, put it that way. And choose the best system.”
U.S. AI firms are bringing investments to other countries like Singapore, where Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office. The city-state says it is also considering joining China’s AI organization.
In Saudi Arabia, the AI startup Humain unveiled in September a platform built on an open model by a Chinese AI company. The kingdom also has a deal with Nvidia to expand AI computing with its advanced chips.
France, one of the most ambitious AI developers aside from the U.S. and China, is attempting to go its own way with its startup Mistral, whose new model released this month outperforms some advanced Chinese models.
Japan is closely aligned with the U.S. on strategic and security issues, including advanced semiconductors, trusted AI and standards. But it will not reject the more affordable Chinese AI models for “lower-risk applications,” said Takahiro Tsuchiya, a professor at Kyoto's University of Foreign Studies.
For countries like the U.K. and Germany which have substantial economic and military capacity but no self-developed powerful frontier AI models of their own, aligning with the U.S. may be vital for their access to data centers and chip deals with U.S. companies, said Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Essentially, their access to advanced AI systems “depends on the whims of policymakers in Washington and Beijing,” they said, while those countries may have limited influence over AI’s future.
China, meanwhile, has been closing the technology gap with the U.S. when it comes to chipmaking and advanced AI capabilities, but it still trails top U.S. technological capabilities, at least for now.
Also, Beijing's open-source approach allows countries to be less reliant on the U.S., and China has been providing funding for developing countries to develop their own AI ecosystems, said Alberto Lemma, a research fellow at the think tank ODI Global.
To date, China has provided official sector grants and loans for project and activities that use or enable AI technologies in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, according to the AidData research lab at William & Mary, a public university in Virginia. Some top recipients include Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon, and Kenya. Public perceptions are also changing. Recent study results from Pew Research Center have shown that people in middle-income countries are becoming more positive and trusting of China when it comes to AI and the technology’s regulation.
All things considered, many countries “don’t want to pick a side ... because there are advantages and disadvantages to each technology stack,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Most countries may eventually lack a good option since they cannot compete on building AI frontier models, but “every country in the world in some way or another is thinking about AI sovereignty," he said. After all, “maybe no other country than the U.S. and China can really build these very large, powerful models.”
Tang reported from Washington.

articles.title_orig: N. Korean leader Kim returns after visit to China border city: state media
articles.title_zh: N. Korean leader Kim returns after visit to China border city: state media
articles.content_orig:
One-day trip comes weeks before Apec forum in China, with Trump and Putin set to attend. Trump has also said he wants to meet Kim again
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, with both sides underlining their traditional friendship and calling to boost cooperation.
He was welcomed and accompanied on his trip by Wang Huning, China’s fourth-ranked official, according to state news agency Xinhua.
Wang called on the two countries to expand people-to-people exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, as well as “strengthen strategic communication and coordination, and foster a peaceful and stable external environment”, so as to safeguard their “respective sovereignty, security and development interests”.

articles.title_orig: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care
articles.title_zh: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care
articles.content_orig:
Xuan feeds Xu liquid food spoonful by spoonful, taking an hour per meal, and turns her over 10 times daily to prevent bedsores
A woman in eastern China has been devotedly caring for her daughter-in-law for 17 years, ever since she fell into a vegetative state, moving social media users.
The younger woman, surnamed Xu, fell into a vegetative state in 2009 after being struck by a truck in her village in Qingyun county, Shandong province. The accident happened just one month after she got married, Shandian News reported.
Since then, her mother-in-law, Xuan Fengying, has cared for her around the clock.
“She married my son, so she’s my child. How could I abandon her?” the 68-year-old Xuan was quoted as saying.

articles.title_orig: How Much Would It Cost To Build A PC That Can Compete With The PS5 Pro?
articles.title_zh: How Much Would It Cost To Build A PC That Can Compete With The PS5 Pro?
articles.content_orig:
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
In a long-surviving Rockstar Games tradition, "Grand Theft Auto VI" will make its debut on consoles before PC. Since you'll be spending loads on a new console to play it anyway, maybe you'd prefer using the extra time before its PC release to build one that will be able to run Rockstar's new masterpiece once it's available, and in the meantime, run other games at the level of the PS5 Pro. How much will this endeavor cost you, though?
Let's start with the GPU. The RTX 5060 Ti is one of the graphics cards that can technically outperform the PS5 Pro in terms of raw power. Yet, it's often cited by many as the closest equivalent to the PS5's fully custom AMD GPU. For the CPU, the AMD Ryzen 7 3700X is more or less the same, so that goes in the shopping cart. The PS5 Pro has 16GB of DDR6 RAM (shared between the CPU and GPU) with an extra few GBs for the system. For your PC, it's more logical to simply get 16GB of DDR4 RAM to be on the safe side and edge out the PS5 Pro. These three components alone will set you back by approximately $1,000 (around $750 for the GPU , and $118 and $148 for the RAM and CPU, respectively).
Unfortunately, the seemingly less important things will add up, as you can see in these examples. For the CPU, you'll need a motherboard with an AM4 socket, which is around $100 . A 750W power supply will cost $90 and keep you in the clear. You also need a 2TB SSD for storage, which will run you about $220 , and you can get a solid case and three case fans for around $100 . Put it all together, and your build will cost in the neighborhood of $1,530 — around $50 less than the $1,580 console.
You can save more money by ditching Nvidia and going all in on an AMD build. Though some argue that AMD's RX 7700 XT is the closest to PS5 Pro , real-world benchmarks show that you'll need at least an RX 9060 XT, which, thankfully, costs $200 less than the RTX 5060 Ti. With other components, you really don't want to cheap out, but it's absolutely amazing that you could technically build a PC for around $1,300 that will deliver the same performance as the PS5 Pro, and even outperform it in some games (easier hardware optimization on consoles is still a factor to consider).
What if that's still a bit too steep? In that case, building something closer to the regular PS5 will help you tighten your budget significantly. Starting with the GPU, you can grab the RX 6600 XT for about $350 to match the base PS5 , and feel free to bump down the storage to 1TB to get about the same amount as on Sony's console. That alone will bring down the price of the build to $1,050, as you can buy a 1TB SSD for around $150.
The latter build will be more than enough to run the latest games on high settings. However, be warned that the RX 6600 XT struggles with ray tracing. Yet, you'll be able to get 60FPS in most recent titles running on high settings. In the end, building a PC can be a hassle, and if you just want to play some games without much thought about performance, then maybe you'll be fine with a laptop that costs the same as a PS5 Pro – or perhaps less, considering that the PS5 Pro's price has gone through the roof in 2026.

articles.title_orig: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.title_zh: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
articles.content_orig:
Power lines near the Gravelines Nuclear Power Station in Gravelines, France on Sept. 15
Recent weeks have brought red flag after red flag for investment in AI and the related data center boom. Bond yields soared for AI infrastructure giant CoreWeave, a sign that investors view the buildout as increasingly risky. And Meta’s reporting of negative free cash flow for the quarter to fund its infrastructure buildout while saying it might need to raise even more capital to fund its AI buildout not only hit its own stock but contributed to a price decline across the big tech companies.
These developments raised questions across Wall Street about whether too much is being spent too quickly on data center expansion. How questions over data center investment play out has big implications for how companies and investors approach the future of energy and, by extension, climate . A pullback in the pace of new data centers could ease pressure to build fossil generation, but it would also weaken the commercial case for clean energy technologies that need big, reliable buyers who are willing to pay a premium for power.
Most obviously, a dent in the AI buildout would translate directly into a slowdown in related electricity demand growth. In advanced economies like the U.S., data centers will account for 20% of that growth through 2030. By then, data centers are expected to account for 3% of global electricity demand, according to data from the International Energy Agency.
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
Some climate advocates may initially rejoice at slowing electricity demand. Even as renewable energy expands, grids around the world still rely on fossil fuels. In the U.S. in particular, AI demand has sparked a wave of building new natural gas infrastructure. In the short term, slowing demand would mean lower emissions from the existing system than today’s baseline assumptions and less investment in new natural gas infrastructure.
But a slowing data center build out leaves less mature technologies at risk. From advanced geothermal to new ways of producing nuclear power, big tech companies have been willing to pay more to lock in reliable power sources, thereby accelerating the market for these new efforts. Even unproven technologies like nuclear fusion have received a big financial boost from tech firms speculating that they might help solve their power challenges and give them a competitive leg up in the AI race. In a tighter financial environment with lower projected electricity demand, both the incentive and the financial capacity to make bold bets diminish.
To be clear, data centers are not the only source of growing electricity demand. New manufacturing continues to create the need for power. The need for air conditioning has ramped up in many emerging markets, particularly in the Global South, creating new grid pressures. And electric vehicles continue to take off in many markets outside the U.S.
Even as gas remains resilient, much of the power built to meet demand will come from clean sources, including and especially solar and battery storage. Solar is increasingly cost competitive. And this year’s spike in fuel prices—particularly natural gas—has made local power more appealing. But the companies behind growing sectors like air conditioning and EVs are less involved in local power systems and lack the capital to really shape them like the world’s wealthiest tech companies have. In short, clean energy will take a hit without the backing of big tech.
It’s too soon to tell whether, in the long run, this week’s AI infrastructure recalibration will be a blip in time or part of a much broader realignment. But it’s something that anyone invested in clean energy and climate should be watching closely.

A man in Germany was arrested on suspicion of arson this week after he allegedly set fire to a mountain retreat built for Adolf Hitler.
The fire broke out at the Eagle’s Nest in the Bavarian Alps on Friday evening, and firefighters battled the flames against strong winds.
The 33-year-old suspect is a German citizen who showed signs of mental illness and was taken to a psychiatric facility, authorities said.

The Eagle's Nest, built for Adolf Hitler in the Bavarian Alps, burns early Saturday. (Bergerlebnis Berchtesgaden via AP)
But they aren’t ruling out a political motive for the arson due to its notorious history.
He was seen heading down the mountain on a motorcycle.
The Kehlsteinhaus, as it’s called in Germany, is more than 6,000 feet above sea level and accessible by an elevator during the day for tourists.
The building has operated as a seasonal restaurant and tourist attraction since 1952, and has an exhibit on its history .
MASSIVE FIRE DESTROYS 400-YEAR-OLD FOOD MARKET, LEAVING HISTORIC LANDMARK IN RUINS

He did frequent his Berghof residence in the same area, which was blown up after the war.
"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, told reporters at Eagle’s Nest. "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

He added: "It is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

articles.title_orig: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
articles.title_zh: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
articles.content_orig:
Escalating war rhetoric from Iran, the United States and Israel, coupled with military movements across the region, has heightened fears of another conflict, as Iranians debate online whether war could bring political change or deepen the country's crises.
Iranian social media users are closely following statements by US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as well as diplomatic and military movements across the region.
Many view the developments as possible signs of an impending US-Israeli attack.
A central debate is whether another war could bring down the Islamic Republic or simply inflict further damage on Iran.
Those supporting military action describe war as a necessary evil to end the political system, arguing that previous attempts to bring about change have failed.
Opponents warn that another conflict could destroy energy infrastructure and refineries, deepen economic hardship and leave Iranian society in an even worse position.
“We are inside Iran and face all kinds of financial, security and social problems, but we are willing to pay the price to end this nightmare,” one user wrote.
Another user wrote: “This uncertainty is really a thousand times worse than war. We cannot even plan a trip, let alone make decisions about work, education or running a business.”
Others strongly rejected that view.
“War brings destruction, chaos, disease and so many other problems,” one user wrote. “The outcome will not necessarily be what you imagine. It could be much worse than things are now.”
Another highlighted the vulnerability of people without secure salaries, who could lose their livelihoods if fighting disrupted economic activity.
One user summed up the conflicting attitudes they had encountered.
“I have seen many people in Iran waiting for an attack so that things can finally be settled… and others who wanted an agreement to be reached,” the user wrote. “Feelings differ, but everyone is tired of this situation.”
Some are urging others to stock up on water, food and medicine and keep cash on hand. Others warn people living near military or government facilities to consider leaving.
Users have also expressed concern for elderly people, those with illnesses and people living alone.
Hardliners push for confrontation
Ultra-hardline voices have also expressed enthusiasm for military confrontation, but for very different reasons.
They argue that negotiations with Washington have merely given Iran's adversaries time to regroup and prepare for a stronger attack.
Some have sharply criticized officials who pursued diplomacy and called for Iran to launch a pre-emptive strike if war appears imminent.
“Why shouldn't Iran start the war this time instead of always waiting to be caught off guard?” one user wrote.
Another argued that Iran did not need nuclear weapons to inflict serious damage on its adversaries.
“We don't even need an atomic bomb to retaliate,” the user wrote, arguing instead for strikes on nuclear power plants in Israel and the United Arab Emirates.
The calls for confrontation reflect a very different political outlook from anti-government users hoping outside military action could bring down the Islamic Republic.
But both illustrate how repeated rounds of fighting and failed diplomacy have led some on opposing sides of Iran's political divide to see another war as preferable to the current uncertainty.
Parents prepare for the worst
Parents' concerns about children's safety have intensified following the deaths of more than 100 schoolchildren in a US attack on Minab at the beginning of the recent war.
Some are urging families to keep children home from school if the likelihood of an attack increases. Others are discussing plans to collect children from schools and move them to safer locations as quickly as possible if fighting resumes.
An Instagram post featuring a firefighter has attracted particular attention. The firefighter said that while inspecting safety arrangements at a girls' high school, a school official told them instructions had been issued to prepare identification tags for students.
On Friday, an Education Ministry spokesperson denied that such measures were being implemented and accused “enemies or ignorant individuals” of spreading fear.
One user said they had checked with relatives in Tehran and concluded that the reports were accurate, claiming families they contacted had requested identification tags and were awaiting their delivery.
Fear of another internet blackout
The prospect of another shutdown of international internet access is adding to the anxiety.
Users fear authorities could cut international connectivity immediately if hostilities resume. The prospect is particularly troubling after previous shutdowns made it difficult to contact relatives and access reliable information.
One user recalled that during the war in June last year, the internet was cut several days after fighting began. When war broke out again at the end of February, the shutdown came within hours.
“Now, instead of checking the news in the morning, I open Google's domain to see whether it loads,” the user wrote, “so I can find out whether the war has started.”
Mike Waltz told the Financial Times that Washington still wanted Tehran to return to negotiations and reach what he called a “meaningful agreement” on its nuclear program, but acknowledged the standoff could continue without a deal or a return to prewar shipping levels through the Strait of Hormuz.
“The president and the US Navy can maintain this blockade for the foreseeable future,” Waltz said, adding that the administration was continuing to tighten economic pressure.
He said the US would not consider its objectives achieved until Iran’s highly enriched nuclear material had been dealt with and an agreement reached over domestic uranium enrichment.
Trump considers renewed strikes after midterms
The comments come as Trump is considering several days of renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms, The Atlantic reported, citing officials and people familiar with the discussions.
Potential targets include Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities, according to the report. One outside adviser told the magazine that US economic pressure was working and that additional strikes could push Iran closer to collapse.
An official and another person familiar with the talks said Trump had initially hoped Tehran would return to negotiations before the election, but that had not happened.
US officials stressed that no decision had been made on whether to resume strikes after November 3. The Atlantic said some officials also saw uncertainty over Washington’s next move as a way of keeping Tehran under pressure.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for another round of strikes before Israel’s election, according to the report, but Trump has so far declined to authorize a new attack before the US vote.
Washington and Tehran trade competing Hormuz messages
The military pressure is unfolding alongside sharply different accounts from Washington and Tehran over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump said on Thursday that more oil had moved through the strait over the previous week than at any point before the war, attributing the increase to the US blockade.
“More oil came out of the Hormuz Strait over the last week than at any time previous, including before the war,” Trump told a campaign rally in Iowa. “That’s because of the blockade.”
He said the blockade had stopped Iran from exporting its own oil and again argued that US military action had destroyed Tehran’s nuclear enrichment capacity.
IRGC says US pushed away from the strait
Iran, however, presented a very different picture on Friday.
IRGC Navy commander Ali Ozmaei said US forces had been pushed hundreds of kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz and no longer had a place there.

articles.title_orig: ‘The worst thing we could do is pick one over the other’: an Australian economist on why US-China competition is ‘a gift’
articles.title_zh: ‘The worst thing we could do is pick one over the other’: an Australian economist on why US-China competition is ‘a gift’
articles.content_orig:
John Edwards reflects on a changing world, economic statecraft and an AI-led manufacturing revival
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
John Edwards wants us to chill out about China.
A former top economic adviser to Paul Keating in the early 1990s, Edwards has been a major figure in the private and public sectors over the past three decades.
Now a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, Edwards has published a new paper titled Overhaul: How Australia can adapt to a changing world economy.
In the paper, Edwards writes that the “vigorous competition and intermittent antagonism” between China, our major economic partner, and the US, our traditional ally and security partner, has long been “mostly a source of anxiety” for Australians.
Yet, Australians should see US-China competition as “a gift”, and we are well placed to become a more prosperous nation over the next 25 years – as long as we play our cards right.
One is that we need to recognise that the US and China will still be the major economies in 25 years. They’re not going to go away. It’s not a race between the two that either can win.
So Australia is in a peculiar position of having a very strong cultural and security relationship with the US, and a very strong economic relationship with China, and we ought to regard that as a great advantage to have such strong links with the two major global economies.
And rather than being anxious about this, we should celebrate it – bearing in mind that the worst possible outcome for Australia is for China and the US to become more adversarial.
It’s better for smaller countries to have two big players than one, and that’s the circumstance in which we find ourselves. So the worst thing we could do is pick one over the other.
So another one is to re-energise our economic statecraft; this is an area where we used to be very good.
In recent years – recent decades – we’ve become dominated by national security considerations, almost to the exclusion of economic statecraft.
[We need] more openness to foreign investment.
On some levels we are. You do see headlines [about how] we’re preparing ourselves for a conflict with China.
I mean, Europe’s not preparing itself for a conflict with China. Canada’s not preparing itself for a conflict with China, and Indonesia’s not, and Malaysia’s not. I’m not sure Japan is, although it says it is. India’s not.
Why would we be preparing for a conflict with China? I think it’s a relatively superficial understanding of our actual position in the world.
Well, I think we do need to be careful to maintain the balance of our relationship with China.
We certainly should not meekly accept China’s sanctions on us, but we should also be very careful not to go out of our way to provoke them.
We have a tiny manufacturing sector. We can almost start from scratch.
We have certain advantages that would become more apparent if we overcome the problem of our labour costs, which are quite high.
[High labour costs] is a good thing – it’s a reflection of the fact that we’ve got high living standards, but they’re an impediment to global manufacturing competitiveness.
And what AI offers us, for the first time in our history, is a way around it. It says we can recommence manufacturing with AI-enabled robots.
But we have to recognise that if we’re going to restore a manufacturing sector in Australia, it’s highly likely to be part of a supply chain that, one way or another, touches on China.
If there’s going to be foreign investment in Australian manufacturing, then it’s highly likely they’ll either be Chinese or influenced by China, and we have to recognise that fact.
No, it’s not a jobs-rich industry, and there’s no way manufacturing is going to be jobs-rich in the future.
There is a lot of short-termism in our comprehension of what’s happening in the global economy, and it’s useful every now and then to step back and say, ‘Well, actually, what has been going on?’
And as I say, if you look at the last 25 years, calamitous though they were in many respects, the economic outcomes were pretty good and replicated those of the previous 50 years.
I think there are several things going on. In the case of the US, it’s the awareness that China now matches it in economic weight.
The other thing in the US is just unchecked growth of inequality, and particularly the outstanding growth in the wealth, power and prestige of the top 1% of the population. It’s unprecedented.
In Europe, it’s slow growth in living standards compared to a lot of other places, including Australia. A discordant migration story.
But a generally gloomy view is not true of India, and not true of China or of many other countries which have done extremely well.
I just can’t account for it, because we’ve done well.
We’ve got problems now. We’ve got high inflation, which we need to restrain. And we’ve got very low growth in productivity – it’ll be a very good thing when that revives.
But in terms of our long-term outlook, it’s pretty good.
I guess it is. But it’s basically a supply-side issue which we’re beginning, I think, to address.

articles.title_orig: How one man became the unsung hero of the internet during a cyber-security scramble
articles.title_zh: How one man became the unsung hero of the internet during a cyber-security scramble
articles.content_orig:
For more than 20 years, Ondřej Surý has been quietly helping to keep websites around the world running securely, largely in his spare time.
He voluntarily maintains software for two of the most popular versions of Linux, a free operating system similar to Windows, which are often used on web servers.
Typically, this involves keeping them up-to-date with the latest version of PHP, a programming language which underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
This week, he became very busy indeed.
With the help of AI, two major cyber-security flaws were identified in the programming language, leading the PHP Foundation to release fixes.
But average folk may struggle to understand how to install these onto their systems - so Surý, for free, dropped everything to convert the fixes into packages, which can be easily installed without expertise.
"The feeling is like I am responsible for all these people and I can't fail them," he told BBC News.
The vulnerabilities in PHP sparked an international scramble to install security updates, amid fears that cyber criminals could exploit the gaps.
Surý is one of a small number of developers whose work helps make those updates available.
And while keeping the internet secure might sound like a full-time occupation, it isn't actually his day job.
He works as director of DNS engineering at Internet Systems Consortium, a US non-profit organisation.
But in his spare time, he has spent more than two decades voluntarily maintaining PHP software packages for the Linux versions Debian and Ubuntu.
He takes the source code released by the PHP project and turns it into packages which website operators can easily install on their servers.
When asked how it felt to be described as one of the people who helped "save the internet" this week as some online put it, his response was modest.
"It's kind of fulfilling because I sense my work has a purpose," he said.
"At the same time, I feel that not enough credit has been given to other people who has been part of this, like the PHP project people."
But he also acknowledged the weight that comes with his role.
Surý had been given advanced warning about the vulnerabilities by the PHP project, but when information about the weaknesses leaked online, the planned release was brought forward and things started ramping up.
"I got aware that this is quite severe and I don't have that much time to prepare the packaging of the PHP that I provide to people," he said.
Despite the urgency, he said he was confident that his experience and preparation would allow him to get the job done.
Other developers around the world were also working to ensure the patches could be distributed - highlighting just how much of the internet's essential infrastructure sometimes depends on dedicated developers.
Surý said this week had prompted an outpouring of support from people who relied on his software packages.
He revealed that he received more than $10,000 (£7,470) in donations in just a few days.
"This week is basically about a year's worth of the contributions that I got before," he said.
He said major technology companies should take more responsibility for supporting the open source software they depend upon.
"I think they should be more responsible," he said.
"If you just take and don't give back then it will backfire."
Surý has also been considering what would happen if he could no longer maintain the software packages himself.
He said colleagues at software company Freexian could take over, but they do not yet have the same accumulated experience.
"Yes, that's pretty much true," he said, when I asked him whether much of the responsibility ultimately rested with him.
But he is concerned that AI may be dramatically accelerating the discovery of security vulnerabilities, helping both cyber criminals and those trying to stop them.
"I think this is was the most severe incident in years, but I think that because of the AI capabilities are getting better in the cyber security, this might not be an isolated incident," he said.
"And people should be prepared to act this quickly more often because incidents like this might happen in the future - in the near future."

articles.title_orig: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.title_zh: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.content_orig:
Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.
The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.
The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.
This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.
As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.
Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.
National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.
With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.
To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.
From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.
For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.
But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.
Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.
When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.
The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."
It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.
Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."
Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.
The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.
This is a row that is playing out in the election.
There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.
Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.
Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.
All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.
A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.

articles.title_orig: Arrests in Barcelona after 'anti-system' rioters loot shops, set fires
articles.title_zh: Arrests in Barcelona after 'anti-system' rioters loot shops, set fires
articles.content_orig:
A total of 100 people were arrested in Barcelona on Saturday evening after hooded demonstrators who participated in an anti-establishment rally looted shops and set fire to street furniture around the city's central Plaza de Catalunya.
Núria Parlon, the interior minister for the Spanish region of Catalonia , said around 25% of those arrested were minors. More than 30 fires were set and 14 stores vandalized or looted in a part of town popular with tourists and weekend shoppers, she added.
Demonstrators were called in social media posts to a movement "against the system." The posts also used the slogan "Institut Indignats," a translation of the movement "Lyceés Indignés," which was used to rally students who have protested in France in recent weeks. In English, the phrase translates as "Indignant High School Student."
Social media videos show people trapped inside shops, including department store El Corte Inglés, after shutters were lowered to prevent looting . Other posts showed hooded demonstrators dressed in black kicking in shop windows and making off with goods, in some cases encouraged by online viewers.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said acts of vandalism in the city "will not go unpunished," including legal consequences for the guardians of any minors involved.

articles.title_orig: Six Flags Will Add Seatbelts to Some Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
articles.title_zh: Six Flags Will Add Seatbelts to Some Roller Coasters After Rider’s Death
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags will add seat belts to Goliath and other roller coasters with similar restraints following the death of a man who fell from the ride at Six Flags Over Georgia earlier this month.
The company’s CEO said in a statement Friday that Goliath remains closed pending safety reviews and clearances following the death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old Atlanta resident and “cherished member” of a public charter school, who fell from the coaster on October 12 . Several other parkgoers were injured, including four minors, police said.
In a statement addressed to guests and passholders, Six Flags President and CEO John Reilly said the company is reinforcing safety precautions across its parks, including installing seat belts on the Goliath, and has engaged independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across its attractions.
Goliath, a 3.5-minute ride reaching 70 mph and a height of 200 feet, features a waist restraint but does not have an over-the-shoulder harness . The addition of seat belts marks a significant change to the ride’s restraint system as investigators continue to examine what happened.
“Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” Reilly said, adding that the company is committed to evaluating the findings and taking appropriate action.
“Safety also depends on the dedicated teams who operate and maintain our attractions every day. Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience, with additional instruction and evaluation provided as necessary,” he continued.
Goliath and eight other rides at five additional Six Flags parks remain temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution, according to the company. Six Flags said its parks remain open, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across its properties.
Preliminary information gathered at the scene from witnesses and employees indicated Kariem had been ejected from the ride, the Cobb County Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit said. He struck other riders before falling beneath the roller coaster, where he was found “unresponsive and not breathing,” police said in a statement.
One witness, CiCi Nelson , told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when a cart pulled up with an empty seat and other riders in hysterics.
She said the safety bar on the empty seat appeared loose, and another young passenger appeared to be covered in blood and injured. Emergency personnel quickly arrived, and she and others were asked to evacuate the area.
The announcement of the new seat belt installations follows the reopening of Six Flags Over Georgia last Friday, when visitors returned for the park’s annual Halloween Fright Fest events. Goliath remained closed as families entered the park, and officials offered no new findings about the fatal incident.
What we know about the fatal roller coaster incident at Six Flags Over Georgia
Georgia authorities are investigating the death, reviewing evidence, equipment and documentation to determine whether state safety requirements were followed, according to a statement last week from Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King. Cobb County police are assisting state and park officials.
CNN has reached out to Cobb County, Cobb County Police and the Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner for an update on the investigation into Kariem’s death and comment on Six Flags’ plans to add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters.
As the investigation remains underway, CNN analysis has revealed alleged maintenance issues and guest injuries at several Six Flags parks.
CNN’s review of safety records from 2016 through 2026 found that Goliath appeared to have passed annual state safety inspections. The coaster’s most recent inspection, on March 16, reported no violations, deficiencies, citations or red tags, according to King. A separate inspection report earlier this year noted that bushings, which are components that help reduce vibration, on the coaster needed replacement, according to CNN affiliate WSB.
“I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “As CEO of Six Flags, I take that responsibility personally.”
CNN’s Isa Mudannayake, Karina Tsui, Isabel Rosales, and Julianna Bragg contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:

Almost 1,000 people have been arrested during protests across France, the interior minister says, as clashes erupt after a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations
In Porte de Vincennes, Paris, protesters threw objects towards the police, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux
Police fired tear gas in cities including Lyon and Nantes as hundreds of thousands took to the streets across France - 110,000 protesters marched in Paris alone, police say

Today's marches follow last weekend's riots and looting that saw more than 2,700 arrested across France - why are people protesting?
Elsewhere in Europe, protests have also been taking place today in Brussels, Rome and Milan
Edited by Matt Spivey and Charlotte Hadfield, with Nick Beake and Mark Lowen in Paris
Jacob Phillips Live reporter
Protesters take cover behind a plywood board as French riot police use a water canon in Paris
French police have fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse protesters as clashes broke out following a day of mostly peaceful demonstrations across France.
Almost 1,000 people have been arrested, according to officials, as an estimated 410,000 people rallied across the country. The unions put the number at about 800,000.
In Paris, our reporterâs eyes were filled with tear gas as a protest turned ugly in the French capital, with objects thrown towards police.
In Marseille, barricades and rubbish bins were set alight, while protesters ripped boards from a shop to build a street barricade in Bordeaux.
Meanwhile in southeastern city of Grenoble, hundreds of masked individuals carried out acts of vandalism and attacked police âwith mortars and projectilesâ, according to officials.
Officials have so far managed to avoid a repeat of last weekend's rioting and looting, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history. More than 2,700 people were arrested following the mass disorder on 17 October.
We are ending our live coverage now, but you can read more about the French protests here .
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.
A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as demonstrators were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.
Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.
Protesters face police during the demonstrations in Marseille
The mayor of Marseille says several groups attempted to loot different parts of the city on Saturday.
BenoÃ®t Payan asks people in Marseille to "remain cautious" and to work with police and the emergency services.
French media reports 51 people were arrested in the city including 20 adults, citing the region's prefecture.
Sarah Rainsford Southern Europe correspondent, in Milan
A major security operation including the deployment of 100s of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering for most of the day in Milan .
It was part of the governmentâs zero tolerance response after violent scenes in the city last week when some demonstrators set fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
There were protests today elsewhere in Italy , including skirmishes with police in Bologna , where water cannons were used, and Turin where protesters also burned a picture of the prime minister.
But early this afternoon a man described as the 'brains' behind the 17 October Movement (M1710) which had called today's protests was identified and taken in for questioning by police.
The mysterious movement had promised to post details on social media of where to gather in each city - in order to avoid the police - but its social media accounts were never updated.
Here in Milan , that left would-be protesters lost for what to do, or where to go, and easily outnumbered and outmanoeuvred by police and paratroopers.
We saw groups - mostly teenagers - being stopped and searched on a massive scale, with police checking their bags and documents.
Later in the evening, a crowd of demonstrators marched peacefully through the city, ending outside the Polytechnic University.
âThe cost of living," a group of young women there told the BBC, when asked why they were protesting - mentioning high rents and the cost of fuel. âWe can barely make it to the end of the month.â
As we've been reporting , away from France, protests have also been taking place across other parts of Europe today.
Italian media report that police arrested nine people and detained 371 people, including 110 minors, following demonstrations in Italy.
The footage below shows police firing a water cannon at protesters in central Rome.
Nearly 1,000 people have been arrested during demonstrations across France today, with that number expected to rise, according to Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez.
The photos below show the scenes that took place in Paris and Marseille this evening.

Around 11,500 people gathered in Rennes, France, on Saturday despite the demonstration being banned, the prefecture covering the area says.
In a statement it says "several thousand people" were hostile towards police officers as they marched towards the city centre, despite organisers saying they would disperse the crowd.
It says security forces confronted "particularly violent individuals", including some who fired projectiles.
A water cannon and two armoured vehicles were deployed to push back protesters and dismantle barricades created in several streets, the statement says.
The prefecture adds that 52 arrests had been made.
There has been a "tense end to the demonstration" in Toulon in southern France following several clashes between protesters and police officers, the local prefect has said.
The prefect says smoke bombs and projectiles were thrown while flares were fired from boats.
Around 150 people then gathered in the city and set fire to garbage bins before dispersing, the prefecture adds.
An order banning people from gathering was issued.
In the last few hours 55 people have been arrested including 33 minors. Around 11 people are in police custody.
Two officers and two protesters were injured during the clashes.
A woman tries to protect herself from tear gas next to police officers during a protest in Nice
In Nice, where demonstrations had been banned today, more than 2,000 people gathered to protest, police say.
PrÃ©fet des Alpes-Maritimes says during the dispersal of the protest far-right and far-left protesters clashed.
They add 63 people were arrested, two police officers were injured and three protesters sustained minor injuries.
A French prefect "condemns with the utmost firmness" damage in downtown Bordeaux.
Pictures show a statue in the city has graffiti at its base while a coffee shop has had its windows smashed and more graffiti sprayed across its front.
"These acts are unacceptable," says prefect Sophie Brocas, who represents the Nouvelle-Aquitaine and Gironde regions.
"The perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts."

articles.title_orig: More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt
articles.title_zh: More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — I was standing in the middle of the street in east Paris, surrounded by mostly masked protesters , when my throat started suddenly burning. Out of seemingly nowhere, I was coughing uncontrollably and felt my throat closing up. That was the first tear gas fired of the night. I hurriedly reached for the gas mask I’d carried in my backpack the whole day throughout what up to that point had been a large but peaceful march.
Saturday’s protest , the main one in Paris, started at the Porte d’Italie, a largely residential neighborhood on the left bank of the Seine. Police changed the approved route at the eleventh hour Friday night, saying the original one, meant to go from Place de La Bastille through Place de la Nation in central Paris, would be too difficult to secure.
And indeed, along this new route, there were barely any shops for the protesters to loot , as they had famously done the weekend before. Instead were mostly working-class high-rise apartment buildings, where residents, not used to seeing political action in this part of town, came out on their balconies, some with a cigarette in hand, to peek at the tens of thousands marching through.
By the time it reached its end point, after nearly three hours, at Porte de Vincennes, riot and military police were making clear that – unlike the previous weekend where the police response was criticized – they were the ones calling the shots this time, advancing on the crowd whenever it looked like it would get out of control.
And things remained orderly for nearly another hour – people were chanting, some were jumping and dancing – and we wondered whether we should move to see what was happening in other parts of the city.
But then, as many of these peaceful protesters were hopping on the metro to head on home, others were just arriving. And this late crowd looked different. Their faces were covered, gas masks were already on, they weren’t carrying any signs showing which cause they were fighting for and they moved like they had a purpose.
Then it came, a deafening bang that sounded like gunfire. And several more, easily half a dozen, within a few seconds.
Police had unleashed tear gas and sound grenades after the masked rioters hurled rocks and fireworks at them.
The peaceful march that had wound through Paris for hours had suddenly descended into violence, with clouds of smoke engulfing the streets and police struggling to force the masked mob back.

U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.
A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.
The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.
Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June.
Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.
The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.
Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

articles.title_orig: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.title_zh: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.content_orig:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Transport Ministry denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.
The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.
Yemeni authorities said that the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.
The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.
Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of a number of missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi coalition air strikes killed several civilians in Sanaa and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Riyadh has not commented on the alleged raids.
Also on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X that the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.
Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous”, which embody “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.
The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure, and an airbase.
The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July.
Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.
On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said that government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.

articles.title_orig: Secret Russian Funding Revealed in Trump-Putin Energy Scheme
articles.title_zh: Secret Russian Funding Revealed in Trump-Putin Energy Scheme
articles.content_orig:
A multibillion-dollar project to tap into natural gas in Alaska pursued by the Trump administration has been revealed to have secretly received funding from a sanctioned Russian company, according to a report.
Polar LNG, an American energy startup, is seeking to buy Russian technology to extract natural gas from Alaska's North Slope and ship it to allies abroad, portraying the project as a decidedly American undertaking.
But Joel Riddle, who resigned as the company's chief executive last month, told The New York Times that he was misled about the source of the company's funding. He said he had been made to believe that the money came from a firm in the United Arab Emirates, when at least some of it actually came from Novatek, one of Russia's biggest energy companies that is under partial U.S. sanctions.
"It's not only unlawful, but it's not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope," Riddle told the Times.
Yet President Donald Trump's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the project with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin during negotiations last month for a deal to end his war on Ukraine, people familiar with the talks told the Times.
The U.S. sanctions on Novatek mean the Treasury Department would need to approve the use of its equipment in Alaska, and a sanctions bill passed by Congress named after late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina specifically targets Novatek over the company's ties to Putin. Trump waived the law's sanctions last week.
Witkoff and Kushner's willingness to entertain such a deal is a striking example of how Trump and his inner circle have mixed the business of ending a war with the business of making deals, rather than focusing solely on putting an end to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
In the latest twist, Novatek told the Times on Friday that it was moving to acquire "minority shareholder" status in the Polar LNG project, potentially giving a sanctioned Russian energy giant a stake in U.S. gas production.
But even a memo prepared for Polar LNG by outside law firm Baker Botts warned that perceived ties to Novatek could jeopardize licenses and other regulatory approvals, according to the Times. The memo also said federal officials had already expressed concern that one of Polar LNG's investors had links to Novatek and might be acting on the Russian company's behalf.
Ilya Zaslavskiy, a gas industry consultant who studies Russian sanctions and energy issues in Washington, slammed Polar LNG's dealings with Novatek and argued that it should have no place in negotiations over ending the war.
"Any approach by Novatek to transfer technology should be seen as a Kremlin attempt to co-opt U.S. policymakers in order to undermine U.S. foreign policy toward Ukraine and our allies," Zaslavskiy told the Times.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: ‘In three days, we can start writing a different story’: Masses at anti-gov’t rally demand Oct. 7 inquiry
articles.title_zh: ‘In three days, we can start writing a different story’: Masses at anti-gov’t rally demand Oct. 7 inquiry
articles.content_orig:
Justice is elusive, and there are few clearer examples of this than when people who commit acts of sexual violence are given rote tasks as a means of atonement.
Recently, the “Cornell 7” case has inspired new conversations about what accountability and atonement involve. When college administrators investigated a report of sexual violence, some of the alleged perpetrators were reportedly assigned to write “ reflection papers ,” along with other punishments. The writing assignments drew such ire that Cornell issued a statement stating that "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."
I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse , which started when I was 11 years old. Abuse from my step-father went hand-in-hand with punishment. He knew how much I loved words, reading, and writing, and began to use them to discipline me.
Our household was governed by an elaborate set of rules. We were not allowed to speak during dinner without permission. We were required to stand while playing board games. Our bedrooms were inspected every evening, and our beds had to be made with hospital corners.
Any infraction could result in punishment. One of the preferred methods was to require me to write an essay outlining what I had done wrong and how to correct my misdeeds. If I didn't wash the dishes carefully enough, I would have to write an essay about why I needed to take better care when cleaning up after dinner.
Other times, I was ordered to write the same sentence hundreds of times.
If I complained about dinner, I had to write 100 times, “I will appreciate my mother’s cooking.”
If I made fun of one of my siblings, I had to write 250 times, “I will not make fun of my brother.”
And if I resisted attempts to assault me, the punishment could be a thousand repetitions of “I will listen.”
I was being punished for trying to protect myself from the person who was abusing me. In doing so, I learned that writing the correct words was not the same as believing them. I could produce an essay explaining what I might have done wrong and promise to be better, but it didn’t mean that I believed that I misbehaved. It meant that I understood what was required of me. The punishment was complete when the writing was complete, but whether I had learned anything was beside the point.
More than 50 years later, I find myself wondering what we believe an essay can accomplish when it is assigned in response to allegations of sexual violence. Cornell’s disciplinary proceedings have resulted in different sanctions for different students , including expulsions and suspensions. “ Reflection papers ” were among the educational requirements imposed on some students.
But what, exactly, can an assigned essay demonstrate?
An essay can be thoughtful and persuasive; it can express regret, recognize harm, and promise change. But how do we know whether the person who wrote it believes any of what is written? What happens when completing an assignment becomes a substitute for demonstrating genuine understanding or changed behavior?
I have spent my adult life writing, teaching, and interviewing people about their lives. I believe in the ability of language to help us understand ourselves and one another, and I know how easily language can be used to conceal the truth.
My abuser understood the power of words, and used them to dictate the terms of my obedience. He controlled what I was allowed to say. He warned me that no one would believe me and threatened violence against those I love if I spoke out. I believed him, and I remained silent and ashamed.
I was required to write about my smallest infractions while being forbidden, through fear, to speak about the most terrible thing happening in my life. And the person who demanded that I explain my wrongdoing was the person committing the most serious wrongdoing of all.
This is why the relationship between language and power matters so much to me. The person with authority often gets to decide what constitutes an acceptable explanation, a credible account, or a sufficient expression of remorse.
Jane Doe , the young woman at the center of the Cornell case, reported the incident to university police in 2024. Since then, the timing and content of her disclosures have become subjects of intense public scrutiny. Public debate has focused in part on differences between her initial statements and her subsequent allegations.
I cannot speak for her, and our experiences are different. But I understand how fear can determine what someone is willing to reveal, even when she desperately needs help.
There is something troubling about how much we expect words to prove in cases of sexual violence. We scrutinize the accounts of those who report abuse, searching for inconsistencies. Now we are asking those found responsible for misconduct to demonstrate understanding through written reflection.
I believe writing can lead to meaningful change. But an essay is evidence that someone has completed an assignment. It cannot establish whether that person understands the harm they have caused or whether their behavior will change.
Why are we putting so much faith in the words people are required to write, while questioning the words that others struggle to say?

articles.title_orig: Protests spread from Paris to other capital cities across Europe
articles.title_zh: Protests spread from Paris to other capital cities across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Protests over a range of issues have taken place in cities across Europe, from Milan and Madrid to Lisbon and Tirana. Demonstrators are taking to the streets over pensions, housing, education, corruption and opposition to war, reflecting a diverse mix of grievances across the continent.
Despite precautions, bans and heavy policing the protests led to violent clashes in several cities in France - around 2,400 people have been arrested, while nearly 1000 members of the security forces were injured, as well 100 protesters and residents in Paris alone.
Thousands of people rallied for a fresh anti-government protest in the Albanian capital Tirana on Saturday, with police firing tear gas to disperse the crowd. In the latest of several clashes between police and protesters since mid-October, government buildings were attacked and dozens of demonstrators were detained. Authorities said that more than 300 protestors and police have been injured.
Thousands took to the streets in Milan, Rome, Turin, Naples, Bologna and Florence with protester throwing bottles, stones and firecrackers.
Italian police said in a statement they had carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement added.
In Madrid the protesters' key demands include linking pension increases to actual inflation, raising the minimum pension to match the minimum wage, closing the gender pension gap and protecting the public pension system from privatisation.
In Portugal affordable housing is the main demand

articles.title_orig: Washington's message to AI execs: Please shut up
articles.title_zh: Washington's message to AI execs: Please shut up
articles.content_orig:
Bipartisan U.S. lawmakers and other government officials are urging artificial intelligence founders to prioritize safe product development, as executives’ public messaging draws concern in Washington.
AI leaders’ messages have shifted between describing the technology’s potential prosperity and warning of existential dangers, sometimes during the same public event. At the same time, industry leaders have not taken a leading role in persuading Americans about AI’s benefits and potential shared prosperity.
Lawmakers and regulators say the swings contribute to political instability amid an already strong public backlash against the industry. Separately, discussion of digital sentience and global catastrophe has turned an already complicated debate over AI regulation into a moral panic.
The officials’ request is for founders to spend less time talking and more time developing products while ensuring safety.

articles.title_orig: Trump and Rubio escalate rhetoric on possible Cuba action
articles.title_zh: Trump and Rubio escalate rhetoric on possible Cuba action
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with the CIA, the latest ploy in the growing efforts from the Trump administration to remove Cuba's communist regime from power.
"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio wrote Friday on X. "The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."
Shortly afterward, the CIA reposted Rubio's message and a similar call in Spanish for Cubans to work with the agency. A video was posted alongside the message showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.
A strict U.S. embargo and sanctions seeking to put pressure on Cuba's communist government have led to prices of basic goods skyrocketing and decreased access to medical care for its citizens. Cubans reported waiting in bread lines for hours and others reported lining up to see a doctor.
Last week, the U.S. government announced additional economic sanctions on Cuba's state-run bank, saying the institution had ties to Iran.
President Trump said on Friday during a campaign rally in South Florida that "we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran." He was referring to the U.S. Navy warships deployed near the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr. Trump added: "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Cuba's government has pushed back, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla responding Friday on X , saying: "We reject any threats stemming from U.S. ambitions toward Cuba."
Rodriguez Parrilla added: "Our shores are lined with beautiful beaches, but they are also rugged and inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile intentions and a desire for domination."
Olivia  Gazis contributed to this report.
