articles.title_orig: Here's the 'core economic flaw' in the AI bull case as stock and bond trades unravel, according to a top economist
articles.title_zh: Here's the 'core economic flaw' in the AI bull case as stock and bond trades unravel, according to a top economist
articles.content_orig:
Apollo Chief Economic Torsten Slok was on a warpath this past week, issuing a series of warnings about the AI boom as Wall Street retreated from the sector.
On Tuesday, he pointed to the recent slowdown in token spending growth , saying the demand curve for compute is flat and highly sensitive to price changes.
Meanwhile, most companies that are investing in the technology have yet to see significant productivity returns, Slok added, with AI now looking more like a cost center than a growth driver.
“The core economic flaw in the AI bull case is that the marginal cost of producing compute exceeds the marginal benefit it delivers to users, raising questions about claims of unlimited demand for data centers,” he explained. “How much compute and how many data centers are needed depends on the returns firms are able to generate with that compute. So far, the AI payoff for firms has been slow to materialize, implying a growing reluctance to pay for AI services.”
The main determinant in data-center construction models isn’t physical capacity or power, he argued. Instead, it’s the actual price users are willing to pay for compute.
But companies will only pay a high price if it translates to higher revenue growth, bigger profits, or substantial savings—and there its little sign any of those exist at scale, Slok wrote.
“Maybe that will come in the future. Maybe not,” he warned.
On Thursday, he sounded the alarm on “circularity” in token spending . AI companies have already come under scrutiny for financing deals where they provide money or guarantee debt for other companies that are also top customers, raising doubts about how sustainable their growth is.
Slok suggested a similar dynamic exists between AI startups and the venture capital firms that invest in them, saying 80% of the top 1% of AI spenders are VC-backed. In his view, that means startups are paying for their compute bills with venture capital rather than organic earnings.
And on Saturday, he declared AI has “ delivered zero financial payoff ” to U.S. companies outside of the big hyperscalers. While profit margins and revenue per workers are rising for the so-called Magnificent Seven, the rest of the S&P 500 has seen no such improvement.
Echoing the week’s earlier notes, Slok said Corporate America overall doesn’t need the latest AI model—and doesn’t want to pay for it. But even as AI becomes cheaper and commoditized, mainstream companies may have a hard time using the technology to boost financial results.
“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote. “Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”
His series of notes came as AI-related stocks tumbled, especially chip names, with traders doubting how much longer the capital expenditure orgy can go on. A handful of hyperscalers plan to spend an estimated $800 billion this year, with capex next year seen topping $1 trillion.
But AI companies may find that raising all that capital won’t be as easy. Meta has already issued a lot of debt, and announced this week the issuance of a new class of shares, in part to help CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay for a possible wealth tax in California.
With the social media giant planning to spend $135 billion-$145 billion this year, the cost of insuring Meta’s debt against default ​touched a record on Thursday. Five-year credit default swaps widened 7.6 basis points to an all-time high of ​114.79 basis points.
At the same time, smaller AI companies like “neoclouds” have come under pressure. For instance, CoreWeave stock has crashed more than 30% this month, and its five-year credit default swaps have shot up to 1,145 basis points.
The worries don’t end there. S&P’s Global Head for Digital Infrastructure Mark Habib flagged “interconnected financing structures” between hyperscalers and data center projects or smaller AI companies.
“It is ⁠safe to assume that there is more (debt) out there that we are not seeing,” he ​said during a roundtable in London, according to Reuters .
“If it’s not reported, then it’s not part of the disclosure ​by the hyperscalers. Also, if we are not rating the transactions where this liability may accrue, then the fact of the matter is that we might not have the visibility.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear
articles.title_zh: Israeli Settlers Turn a Palestinian Rite Into a Gantlet of Violence and Fear
articles.content_orig:
Heidi Levine, the Washington Post journalist brutally attacked by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank last week, said the terrifying ordeal has only strengthened her resolve to continue covering the plight of Palestinians.
“What hurts me the most is I can now really understand what others have gone through, what Palestinian women, children, men have gone through,” she told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday from Israel, where she’s recovering after being released from hospital the day before.
“I’m an American, I work for the Washington Post, my story is getting a lot of attention around the world, everyone wants to talk to me – but I can’t imagine what it’s like for all the victims that have gone through the same ordeal and are living with the threat of this violence on a daily basis,” she added.
“It actually has strengthened my commitment to continue working to try to make a difference.”
Levine, a veteran photojournalist known for her work in the Middle East, was covering the annual olive harvest in the West Bank when she, a group of Palestinians, and other journalists came under attack. Violence in the West Bank has surged in recent years as settlements have expanded, often backed by Israeli forces; attacks on farmers and communities who rely on the olive harvest for their livelihoods now come on a daily basis.
Initially, Levine said, the harvest began as planned. But then, peering through her telephoto camera lens, she noticed people gathering at a nearby hilltop. They seemed young, some wearing black masks; she could see religious garments and headwear like kippah and tzitzit that she said clearly identified them as Israeli settlers.
Washington Post journalist hospitalized after Israeli settler attack on Palestinian olive harvest in West Bank
Their numbers slowly grew to reach several dozen. They began lighting the olive trees on fire and moving closer. “Then all of a sudden, chaos broke out,” she said.
“There was tear gas, there was gunfire. From what I understand, a man was shot; a Palestinian man was shot in the leg, and the settlers charged forward,” she said.
“I was thrown to the ground … They just kept kicking me and hitting me with sticks, and it just kept going on and on. And then I actually thought, okay, maybe I’ll just play dead and pretend I’m dead, and they’ll stop and they’ll leave me alone.”
Instead, her attackers started ripping her gear off her body – her camera bag, her lenses, her pouch containing her American passport, credit cards, documents and other items.
Then they hauled her to her feet, in a moment that has sparked controversy and debate in the week since videos of her attack emerged. In a statement after the attack, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.”
This, Levine says, was false.
“No, they only stood me up because they couldn’t manage to get everything off my shoulders to rob me, including ripping off my gold necklace that my daughter gave me for my birthday,” she said.
The attack finally halted when journalist Jasper Nathaniel and several others came to Levine’s aid – but the danger wasn’t over. Video footage from that moment shows her rescuers holding her up and trying to escape from the attackers, who continue to throw rocks as they give chase.
“Run, run!” Levine’s rescuers can be heard shouting in a panic.
“I can’t,” she responds weakly. They urge her again: “You have to, come on!”
Speaking to Tapper on Thursday, she described it as “this biblical battle where the Palestinian men, a group of men went in front of me to protect us, me and my rescuers from being attacked again.” Without the Palestinians’ intervention, the whole group “would have been in the same situation as me.”
Even with a flak jacket and helmet on, Levine sustained serious injuries, with a broken rib, a broken vertebra, and a severe finger injury that required surgery, said Nathaniel last week after visiting her in the hospital. When she spoke to CNN, her hand was still heavily bandaged.
Her attack was widely condemned by foreign press, the White House, and some Israeli leaders including President Isaac Herzog. Netanyahu, however, tried to cast doubt on Levine’s attack and said that “serious questions remain.”
Just one day after Levine’s assault, settlers attacked a group of European diplomats visiting the Palestinian Christian town of Taybeh, prompting further outcry from the international community.
On Monday, Israeli police arrested at least 10 suspects for both attacks.
But many Palestinian victims of similar attacks never see justice. Since the olive harvest began on September 27, Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented more than 530 incidents of “settler and soldier violence” – which, beyond outright attacks, also includes the looting of crops and livestock, and destruction of olive trees.
More than a quarter of the violence “occurs in solders’ presence and under their protection,” said Yesh Din.
There has been a dramatic expansion of illegal settler outposts across the West Bank since Netanyahu’s government formed in December 2022 – with more than a third approved by the government. With that expansion, settler violence has also spread into parts of the West Bank that had previously seen little or none.
When asked if she blames Netanyahu and other far-right Israeli leaders like national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for her attack, Levine laughed humorlessly.
“Well, you hear their rhetoric, right? You hear their speeches. I’ve documented their visits in the West Bank, so I think the answer is pretty obvious,” she said, warning that things will only worsen, and that authorities “don’t even know how to handle it.”
“This has been going on for over four decades that I have been covering this region, but I’ve never seen this situation in the West Bank or the situation in Israel at the level that it is today.”

articles.title_orig: Israeli central bank rejects Benjamin Netanyahu’s plan to use crypto to evade sanctions
articles.title_zh: Israeli central bank rejects Benjamin Netanyahu’s plan to use crypto to evade sanctions
articles.content_orig:
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot reacted to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's plan for Israel to make use of alternative financial mechanisms , releasing a campaign video on X/Twitter on Saturday in which the former IDF chief described the plan as an admission that the prime minister had economically "destroyed the country."
"All of our money is at risk," the campaign video said, showing Netanyahu in his earlier Channel 10 interview saying that Israel must "prepare for an alternative economy" amid the myriad of international sanctions facing the country .
The video emphasized the point made by Netanyahu regarding blockchain technology, with the prime minister acknowledging that such digital finances would "certainly" be a portion of his plan.
"I’ve already asked for a plan to be prepared for that,” Netanyahu added during the interview.
Eisenkot 's campaign video referred to the plan as "Bibicoin," concluding that such a finance mechanism would "destroy Israel."
The campaign video further claimed that the alternative system would generate "an economy like North Korea and Iran," noting that it would result in "the end of high-tech , the end of healthcare, the end of security."
"We must not let him (Netanyahu) burn through our savings," it said, questioning how the global high-tech industry could invest in Israeli companies if digital currency were the only method.
Eisenkot also addressed Netanyahu's alternative economy plan in a separate X post, delivered this time as a personal message.
"Netanyahu himself admits that the policy he's leading and wants to lead Israel toward will result in international isolation and economic sanctions that will shake the economy and the market," wrote Eisenkot. "This will be the collapse of our national security."
Also on Saturday, the Bank of Israel responded to the blockchain element of Netanyahu's plan, saying that such digital currencies "cannot be used as a way to circumvent sanctions on Israel."
"The right thing for Israel's economy is to maintain economic relations with our main trading partners and focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," the bank said. "This issue is within the responsibility of the political echelon, and it is appropriate to act to advance it."
Netanyahu responded to the Bank of Israel's comments later on Saturday, sarcastically thanking the bank "for the advice," according to KAN News.
B'Yachad chairman Naftali Bennett also responded to the plan, describing himself as a "high-tech entrepreneur" before explaining that Netanyahu's plan would result in "the destruction of Israeli high-tech, the loss of livelihood for hundreds of thousands of families, poverty for millions of Israelis, a serious blow to tourism and businesses, and putting Israel's security in real danger."
"Netanyahu is placing Israel on a par with Iran, North Korea, and Russia," the former prime minister said. "From here, I turn to the business community and all citizens of Israel: This is not a decree of fate. We do not have to walk into the dark future Netanyahu is drawing for our children with our eyes closed. It is possible otherwise. We have the power to build together a wonderful and strong future for Israel."
Tobias Holcman and Maariv contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Israelis rally against Netanyahu gov’t days before election
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Israelis rally against Netanyahu gov’t days before election
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Israelis are protesting against the government and calling for an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks .
Demonstrators rallied in the public plaza known as Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday, three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
Elsewhere in Israel, protesters were also gathering for antigovernment demonstrations, reported Haaretz newspaper.
Taking part were leading figures from opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main centre-right rival.
In Tel Aviv, Eisenkot was greeted by chants of “Who’s coming? The next prime minister”, according to The Times of Israel. The leader of the Democrats, Yair Golan, was also at the rally.
“Masses, masses of masses, flowing in the ‘Democrats’ march from Rabin Square to the Hostages Square – for change, for hope, for r-e-v-o-l-u-t-i-o-n. What energy. This time it’s ours completely!”, Israeli citizen and lawyer Dan Adin posted on X.
Polls ahead of Tuesday’s election suggest a tight race, with Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, in power since late 2022, neck and neck with Eisenkot’s. Neither bloc is currently projected to obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s parliament.
The election could be pivotal in determining whether Israel launches another round of strikes on Iran. Eisenkot is believed to be less inclined to resume military action against Tehran if he becomes Israel’s next prime minister.
However, on most other foreign policy issues, leading Israeli parties and politicians remain united, including in their opposition to the creation of an independent Palestinian state.
Ahead of the protest, the October Council alerted law enforcement to possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
“We have sent an urgent letter to the Police Commissioner following alerts about attempts by entities linked to the coalition to disrupt tonight’s rally,” it wrote on X.
The October Council aims to hold Israeli officials deemed responsible for the October 7 attacks to account and deliver justice for affected families.
Netanyahu’s coalition government, however, has refused demands to establish an independent commission of inquiry. Instead, it has offered to set up a “political” commission. Half of the commission’s members would be appointed by the government, while the remainder would be appointed by opposition legislators.
Opposition leaders have said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

articles.title_orig: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.title_zh: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.
Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .
The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.
The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.
Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.
At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.
Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year,  Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and opera

articles.title_orig: Verizon Apologizes for iPhone Duo Pre-Order Delays, Giving Customers $100 Gift Card
articles.title_zh: Verizon Apologizes for iPhone Duo Pre-Order Delays, Giving Customers $100 Gift Card
articles.content_orig:
Verizon has apologized to customers who pre-ordered the iPhone Duo through the carrier but have since been informed that their delivery is delayed.
In an email sent to affected customers, Verizon said an "unexpected shipping delay" means that iPhone Duo deliveries to some customers will "take a little longer." To make up for the inconvenience, Verizon is offering affected customers a $100 Verizon gift card that can be used online or in-store toward bill payments or merchandise.
"We owe you an apology," said Verizon. "We appreciate your patience and the opportunity to make this right," the company added.
Verizon said customers will receive an email about the $100 gift card next week, and it assured that it is working to fulfill orders as soon as it can.
"Your order is secure, your place in line hasn't changed, and our team is actively tracking your shipment to get it to you as quickly as possible," said Verizon.
MacRumors reader Ryan showed us that he pre-ordered an iPhone Duo from Verizon when pre-orders began on Friday, October 16. Verizon initially quoted him a Friday, October 23 delivery date, meaning he would have received the device on its launch day, but his estimated delivery date has since been revised to Saturday, November 7.
There are many similar examples of Verizon customers with delayed pre-orders across the MacRumors Forums , Reddit , and other social media platforms, with many revised delivery dates now falling in the October 31 to November 14 window.
Some customers who pre-ordered an iPhone Duo through Verizon did receive the device on October 23, so not everyone is impacted.
Last week, Apple said pre-order demand for the iPhone Duo was " nothing short of extraordinary ," with estimated delivery dates on its own online store pushing into late January for new orders. Some lucky customers managed to secure an iPhone Duo on a walk-in basis yesterday, while in-store pickup reservations resumed with little to no availability .
Leading up to the iPhone Duo launch, there were a few reports mentioning that there would be supply constraints due to alleged manufacturing challenges . In any case, getting the device early is proving to be a challenge for some.
In the meantime, Verizon said affected customers can check their iPhone Duo order status on the My Orders page via the My Verizon website or app.

Some may feel this is a step backwards after almost a decade of Face ID on iPhones, but if you wear an Apple Watch, you can use it to unlock your iPhone Duo instead. This way, you don't need to touch the side button at all. It's the closest thing we have to a seamless Face ID experience on iPhone Duo ( at least for now ).
The feature is called Unlock with Apple Watch. It's not new to iPhone, but it works reliably. Note that your Apple Watch needs to be a Series 9 or later, an Ultra 2 or later, or an SE 3. Here's how to turn on the feature and start using it.
From here on, your Apple Watch will handle the authentication – no fingerprint shenanigans required. The swipe up is still needed to get past the Lock Screen, but you can turn off this additional step in Settings .

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo Fails JerryRigEverything's Dusty Durability Test
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo Fails JerryRigEverything's Dusty Durability Test
articles.content_orig:
Apple's iPhone Duo has failed JerryRigEverything's latest durability test . Despite its IP68 dust-resistance rating, dust entered the hinge through several ingress points, overwhelming the magnets that hold the phone shut. The bend test then left a permanent green line across the inner display, before the screen became unresponsive.
The outer screen with Ceramic Shield 2 scratched at level 7 on the Mohs scale, but the inner screen only managed level 2, although credit was given for its matte nano-texture coating making marks "magically disappear." Alas, it wasn't enough to earn a pass. "I've been testing these folding phones since the first generation seven years ago – most do survive," said Nelson. "The iPhone Duo did not." articles.title_orig: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.title_zh: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.content_orig:
Almost the entire management team of the US$25 billion US gas project Polar Train LNG has left the company following allegations of undisclosed financing and control by Russia's Novatek.
Details : The Financial Times reported that the company's former chief executive, Joel Riddle, raised concerns about potential violations of US sanctions.
Polar Train LNG is developing a gas export terminal in northern Alaska. The project was launched in March with a plan to use a partially constructed Novatek terminal and relocate it to Alaska. The company applied to the US Treasury Department for permission to negotiate with the Russian group but has yet to receive approval.
Riddle said he discovered that Novatek was already financing the project and directing its operations before the necessary approvals had been obtained. He resigned in September, after which chief financial officer Dan Chandra and other executives also left the company.
"I resigned as chief executive of Polar LNG because I felt uncomfortable that the Russian company Novatek was financing and ultimately controlling the strategic direction of the company," said Riddle.
He initially believed that the funding was being provided by Gentry Beach, an investor with ties to Donald Trump's family, and Abu Dhabi-based company Tech Wave. Riddle said he later discovered that Beach had not invested in the project and was neither a shareholder nor an executive.
The FT also reviewed WhatsApp messages in which Novatek board member Denis Solovyov discussed financing the project and sought to expedite the transfer of funds to Polar Train LNG.
Polar LNG said Riddle had been dismissed, described him as a "disgruntled employee" and stressed that it was developing the project in compliance with US law.
Novatek said it had agreed to grant Tech Wave the right to use its technology in Alaska and had signed a memorandum with Polar Train in April, when Riddle was still running the company.
According to people who spoke to the FT, the project had featured in talks between Washington and Moscow over business deals that could help bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. The discussions included a potential exchange under which Novatek would provide its expertise for the construction of the Alaska terminal in return for sanctions being lifted on Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project.

articles.content_orig:

Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.
“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said on social media, adding that restoration began overnight and was sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu Is Up for Re-election After Years of War. How Will Voters See Him?
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Is Up for Re-election After Years of War. How Will Voters See Him?
articles.content_orig:
Yoram Ariely left Israel more than thirty years ago and found his way to New York City, where he worked in the food-and-beverage industry. “Mostly juices,” he told me. He eventually retired to Florida, but on Wednesday he was back in New York, sitting in the departures terminal at Kennedy Airport. Ariely is eighty-four years old; when I approached him, he requested that I give him a moment so he could put in his hearing aids. His journey, which had begun that morning, at 7 A.M. , in Sarasota, would end up totalling twenty-four hours. He already looked exhausted.
Ariely, along with others clustered around Gate 18B, waiting to board a non-stop flight to Tel Aviv, was returning to Israel to cast a ballot in the country’s upcoming election—the first time Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will face voters since his contentious effort to neuter Israel’s judiciary; his failure to prevent the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023; and his prosecution of the ensuing war on Gaza, which has shredded Israel’s international reputation and resulted in a warrant for his arrest, for war crimes, from The Hague. “This is the most important election of my lifetime,” Ariely said. (Given that he’s six years older than the Israeli state, his lifetime includes every previous Israeli election.) It will be the first time he’s voted in Israel since moving away.
Around eleven per cent of the Israeli electorate lives abroad. The country does not permit absentee voting, except in rare cases, so any citizen who wants to cast a ballot must return and, on election day, go to the designated polling place for their last official in-country address. This puts a huge price, in time and money—often hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars—on casting a single vote. For Ariely and many like him, it is no deterrent. Eight in ten Israeli voters who live abroad share his view that the upcoming election is “the most crucial” in Israel’s history. Polls show Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition in a dead heat with his chief rival, the centrist Gadi Eisenkot .
Ariely is to the left of Eisenkot politically, but “these considerations must be put aside to give him the majority,” he told me. A man named Hiam Simon, a Jewish American dual citizen who lived in Israel for a stretch in the seventies, piped up from the row of seats opposite us. Ariely, he said, should throw his lot in with the Democrats, a smaller party that would likely become part of Eisenkot’s government, so as to “pull the coalition to the left.”
Ariely was booked in a block of coach seats that had been reserved by the America-Israel Democracy ( AID ) Coalition, a nonprofit based in Pennsylvania that seeks to mobilize Israeli citizens and “concerned Americans” in “preserving the democratic foundations of the state of Israel.” (Simon bought his own ticket, in business class, on the same flight.) The AID Coalition was formed in 2023, after Netanyahu proposed that the Knesset, by majority vote, should be able to overrule Supreme Court decisions. That move sparked enormous street protests in Israel, and alarmed many Israeli citizens overseas.
When the election date was set, this past July—spurred by the legal mandate that Israel hold a parliamentary election at least every four years—the war that Israel and the U.S. had launched against Iran was in its fifth month. Many foreign airlines had paused service to Israel. On those airlines that hadn’t, prices were steep; in May, a round-trip coach seat on our route from New York was running as high as twenty-five hundred dollars. The AID Coalition launched an initiative, Fly&Vote, to help people get back to cast their ballots.
Officially, AID is nonpartisan and assists any eligible voter, irrespective of their political leanings. “We don’t ask,” Batell Blaish-Sultanik, the group’s executive director, told me. Under Israeli election law, it is illegal to provide free or subsidized trips. AID bought blocks of seats on Arkia Israeli Airlines at a commercial rate, securing around a hundred seats on each of five inbound flights before the election and five outbound flights after it. Tickets were then sold to voters at set prices at the lower end of the market rate—topping out at nine hundred dollars each way. Hagai Nassau, an environmental consultant in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, who left Israel as a five-year-old and now sports a graying beard, told me that he had glanced at flights on El Al “and it was, like, three thousand bucks. So I was, like, I’ll do Fly&Vote.”
Of course, for some overseas Israeli citizens, price is no object. Soon after chatting with Nassau at our gate, I spotted Neri Oxman, an Israeli-born architect and the wife of the hedge-fund billionaire Bill Ackman, by a barista counter in the Centurion Lounge. Ackman was sitting nearby. Oxman told me that she saw no option but to return for this election. “It’s so important,” she said, stiffening up like a soldier. “I’m doing my civic duty.” They would be flying El Al.
More than thirty-five thousand overseas Israeli citizens registered to receive information about the AID Coalition’s reserved seats, and for access to a bespoke search engine that had been programmed to find other, affordable options, with complicated itineraries and long layovers. AID estimates that more than sixty thousand will ultimately vote on October 27th.
Netanyahu’s Likud Party clearly regards overseas voters as an obstacle—perhaps even an enemy. While there is scant survey data on the political leanings of Israelis who live abroad, they tend to be secular and more educated, and it is assumed that they skew anti-Netanyahu. More than a quarter of a million people have left the country since 2023. In August, Likud’s attorneys accused the AID Coalition of bribing voters, and brought legal action to try to block its efforts. Three weeks before the election, the chairman of Israel’s Central Elections Committee dismissed the case, but the AID Coalition agreed not to buy more blocks on additional flights. Over the summer, anonymous sources inside Israel’s Transportation Ministry, which is helmed by the populist Likud provocateur Miri Regev, leaked to Israeli media that officials were plotting to reduce capacity at the country’s only major international airport in order to stop anti-Likud voters from arriving. (The AID Coalition has distributed the phone numbers of attorneys to call if any of its passengers run into trouble at passport control.)
Besides the Fly&Vote initiative, several other efforts to bring in voters seem to be under way. A group called Mind-IL is running something called Israeli Science and Academia Week—fifty-nine scholarly conferences, ranging in topics from A.I. to zoology, which all conclude the day before the election. Organizers expect to draw well over three thousand participants, many from overseas. Guli Dolev-Hashiloni, an Israeli-born scholar and activist who is flying in from Berlin, where he is a Ph.D. student in Jewish history, categorized the conferences as “a very good subversive act of Israeli academia that enables people to come back to vote without taking vacation days.” Ran I. Snitkovsky, a member of Mind-IL’s steering committee and a professor at the business school of Tel Aviv University, insisted that any intimation that he and his colleagues were gaming the electoral system was unfair. “We realized there will be a lot of people that want to be here, and we wanted to take advantage of that,” Snitkovsky told me. The result, whatever the intention, will be hundreds of foreign-based academics flying to Israel the week of the election, many on stipends from their universities. Meital Avivi-Reich, an Israeli-born expert on the science of speech perception, who teaches at CUNY , applied for fifteen hundred dollars in funding to present her research at one of the Mind-IL conferences. That will help with the airfare, she told me, but she still plans to stay with her mother and then crash with friends during her shoestring voting-cum-conference

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu Says Israel Mulls Crypto Ahead of Possible Sanctions
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Says Israel Mulls Crypto Ahead of Possible Sanctions
articles.content_orig:
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot reacted to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's plan for Israel to make use of alternative financial mechanisms , releasing a campaign video on X/Twitter on Saturday in which the former IDF chief described the plan as an admission that the prime minister had economically "destroyed the country."
"All of our money is at risk," the campaign video said, showing Netanyahu in his earlier Channel 10 interview saying that Israel must "prepare for an alternative economy" amid the myriad of international sanctions facing the country .
The video emphasized the point made by Netanyahu regarding blockchain technology, with the prime minister acknowledging that such digital finances would "certainly" be a portion of his plan.
"I’ve already asked for a plan to be prepared for that,” Netanyahu added during the interview.
Eisenkot 's campaign video referred to the plan as "Bibicoin," concluding that such a finance mechanism would "destroy Israel."
The campaign video further claimed that the alternative system would generate "an economy like North Korea and Iran," noting that it would result in "the end of high-tech , the end of healthcare, the end of security."
"We must not let him (Netanyahu) burn through our savings," it said, questioning how the global high-tech industry could invest in Israeli companies if digital currency were the only method.
Eisenkot also addressed Netanyahu's alternative economy plan in a separate X post, delivered this time as a personal message.
"Netanyahu himself admits that the policy he's leading and wants to lead Israel toward will result in international isolation and economic sanctions that will shake the economy and the market," wrote Eisenkot. "This will be the collapse of our national security."
Also on Saturday, the Bank of Israel responded to the blockchain element of Netanyahu's plan, saying that such digital currencies "cannot be used as a way to circumvent sanctions on Israel."
"The right thing for Israel's economy is to maintain economic relations with our main trading partners and focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," the bank said. "This issue is within the responsibility of the political echelon, and it is appropriate to act to advance it."
Netanyahu responded to the Bank of Israel's comments later on Saturday, sarcastically thanking the bank "for the advice," according to KAN News.
B'Yachad chairman Naftali Bennett also responded to the plan, describing himself as a "high-tech entrepreneur" before explaining that Netanyahu's plan would result in "the destruction of Israeli high-tech, the loss of livelihood for hundreds of thousands of families, poverty for millions of Israelis, a serious blow to tourism and businesses, and putting Israel's security in real danger."
"Netanyahu is placing Israel on a par with Iran, North Korea, and Russia," the former prime minister said. "From here, I turn to the business community and all citizens of Israel: This is not a decree of fate. We do not have to walk into the dark future Netanyahu is drawing for our children with our eyes closed. It is possible otherwise. We have the power to build together a wonderful and strong future for Israel."
Tobias Holcman and Maariv contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: UK police says letter with claims against Meghan's father was not shared with other law enforcement
articles.title_zh: UK police says letter with claims against Meghan's father was not shared with other law enforcement
articles.content_orig:
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said she is "deeply distressed" by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation over claims he possessed images containing child sexual abuse in his home.
The images were reportedly found in his home in the Philippines after he returned to the U.S. in May, Philippine officials said.
Thomas Markle denied the allegations, calling them "sick lies" and "the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."
London's Metropolitan Police confirmed Saturday that it received a letter in January 2019 containing "a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," the BBC reported . The letter was sent to the force's protection command because of concerns about the duchess's security.
The Met said it passed the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex "for their awareness," but did not share the details with other law enforcement agencies. The force said it is reviewing how it handled the matter and considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, the police watchdog.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan Markle said that she is "deeply distressed" by the news, and that she was first made aware of the claims by the Met Police in 2018.
"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan's statement said. "In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
"I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."
Meghan had said the letter was sent in 2018. A spokesman for the duchess said Saturday that "any discrepancy of a few months" was "an understandable consequence of that passage of time."
Authorities in the Philippines are also investigating. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said national police had secured Markle's computer for a forensic examination, the BBC reported.
The allegations, reported by Mail Online , said Thomas Markle is under investigation after being reported by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
In a statement to Mail Online , the elder Markle said: "I'm shocked, I'm hurt and I'm very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I'm being accused of. It's the worst thing anyone could accuse me of."
He added: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick. I have no idea why Tom [Markle] is trying to destroy me with these lies."
Yahoo has contacted the Met Office and authorities in the U.S. and the Philippines for comment.

articles.title_orig: Jared Kushner’s Lawyer Puts Vanity Fair on Notice Over ‘False’ Claims
articles.title_zh: Jared Kushner’s Lawyer Puts Vanity Fair on Notice Over ‘False’ Claims
articles.content_orig:
Jared Kushner ’s attorney says his legal team has formally put Vanity Fair and its parent company, Condé Nast, on notice over allegations about President Donald Trump ’s son-in-law that the lawyer characterized as “false and defamatory.”
The dispute centers on an excerpt from investigative journalist Matthew Cole’s forthcoming book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East .
The Vanity Fair excerpt alleges that Kushner had access to foreign accounts involving large sums of money during Trump ’s first term.
Kushner has categorically denied the allegations.
Newsweek reached out to Vanity Fair and Cole's representation by email for comment Saturday.
Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and served as a senior White House adviser during Trump’s first administration, from 2017 to 2021.
The allegations concern purported financial arrangements involving countries in the Middle East. According to Cole’s account, Dutch investigators obtained information from Kushner’s compromised phone and uncovered purported financial arrangements involving Middle Eastern governments.
Kushner denies the alleged events occurred.
Cole further alleges that Saudi and Emirati officials arranged for at least $2 billion to be placed in accounts that Kushner could access. The author also alleges that approximately $750 million was transferred into a UAE -linked account on which Kushner was a signatory. Kushner disputes the allegations, and TheWrap said it had not independently verified them.
President Donald Trump has also rejected the report , calling it “a totally false story.”
Kushner has remained involved in U.S. foreign policy after serving as a senior adviser during Donald Trump’s first administration, particularly on Middle East diplomacy. He joined U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in indirect negotiations with Iran in February 2026, talks mediated by Oman that its foreign minister said produced “significant progress.”
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) has accused Kushner of not being properly vetted for the role as one of Trump's top foreign policy representatives.
Kushner was set to travel with Vice President JD Vance and Witkoff in April to Pakistan for talks amid efforts to sustain a U.S.-Iran ceasefire.
In a letter, Kushner’s lawyers disputed the allegations and said the claims at the center of the excerpt amounted to “specific factual accusations of criminal misconduct” that were “categorically false.”
The letter, addressed to Richard A. Bernstein, vice president and deputy general counsel at Advance-Condé Nast, denies a series of allegations individually.
Kushner “was never a signatory to, never had access to, and never knew of any ‘Alpha’ account at First Abu Dhabi Bank,” the lawyers wrote. They also said he did not know of the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, that no “Beta” account was held for him at Israel’s central bank, and that he had no account in Cyprus.
“He never received, controlled, or directed money from any foreign government; never transferred funds to anyone from any such account; and never conditioned any action of the United States government on any benefit to himself,” the letter said.
The attorneys summarized Kushner’s denial in another passage: “There are no accounts and never were.”
The letter also challenged the evidence underlying the allegations, saying that despite repeated requests, Cole had “not provided a single bank statement, account document, or wire record substantiating his accusations.”
Kushner’s lawyers argued that the allegations were particularly implausible given the scrutiny he faced while serving in government, citing media investigations, congressional inquiries and a special counsel investigation.
The letter said Kushner provided more than 30 hours of testimony and filed financial disclosures during his government service, and asserted that none of those proceedings or filings revealed the alleged arrangements.
The attorneys also accused Vanity Fair of publishing the excerpt despite knowing that Kushner disputed the claims. According to the letter, Kushner’s counsel sent Cole and publisher Simon & Schuster letters dated July 30 and August 10 denying the allegations before Vanity Fair published the excerpt.
The October 23 letter demanded that Vanity Fair “immediately take down the excerpt” and preserve documents related to it, while warning that publication had exposed the outlet to what Kushner’s lawyers characterized as “serious legal risk.”
Attorney Chad Mizelle subsequently amplified the warning on X.
“We formally put Vanity Fair and Condé Nast on notice regarding the false and defamatory allegations published about our client, Jared Kushner,” Mizelle wrote in the post.
Mizelle said “serious questions” had been raised about the credibility of the reporting and reiterated the legal team’s objections to the allegations.
Kushner, 45, is a businessman and investor who served as a senior adviser to his father-in-law, Trump, during the president’s first term. Forbes says Kushner worked as CEO of his family’s real estate business, Kushner Companies, from 2008 to 2017 and founded the Miami-based private equity firm Affinity Partners in 2021.
Born January 10, 1981, in Livingston, New Jersey, Kushner is the eldest child of real estate developer Charles Kushner and Seryl Kushner, according to Encyclopaedia Britannica . The publication says he was raised in an Orthodox Jewish family, has three siblings and is the grandson of Holocaust survivors.
Kushner graduated from Harvard University in 2003 and earned a law degree and an MBA from New York University in 2007, according to Britannica . Forbes also lists a bachelor’s degree from Harvard and JD and MBA degrees from New York University among his credentials.
Forbes estimated Kushner’s real-time net worth at approximately $1 billion as of October 24, 2026, identifying real estate and private equity as the sources of his wealth.
Kushner married Ivanka Trump, Trump’s daughter, in 2009, according to Britannica . The couple have three children. Forbes likewise lists Kushner as married with three children.
Mizelle’s statement and the October 23 letter raise the prospect of litigation, but the reporting reviewed does not establish that a defamation lawsuit has been filed.
The letter demands that Vanity Fair remove the excerpt and preserve records related to its publication, potentially setting up a further legal dispute if the parties do not resolve their differences.
Meanwhile, Cole’s book was scheduled for release on October 27.
Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

articles.title_orig: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
articles.title_zh: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
articles.content_orig:
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of Leanne Gregory on Tuesday
The husband of a British woman who died rescuing their sons when they were swept away to sea in the Bahamas says she was a "hero... in life and in death".
Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been snorkelling with her family when the boys were swept away by a strong current, police said.
Although the children were rescued from the water off the island of Bimini on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.
Nathan Gregory said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable for our family".
"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post.
"I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together.
"My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."
Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".
In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".
He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."
The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas said
In a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.
It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.
Mrs Gregory was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.
It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title_orig: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.title_zh: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.content_orig:

American households struggling with elevated living expenses and steep chocolate prices have driven a sluggish start to Halloween candy sales this year.
Figures from market research firm NielsenIQ reveal that candy purchases fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year.
An 11.7% drop in mid-September wiped out early-season sales gains recorded over the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said surging fuel costs have worsened concerns over affordability, curbing demand for treats.
As of Friday, the national average for regular gasoline stood at $4.29 a gallon, up nearly 40% from last year.
"I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food," Costagli said.
"Some of the decisions they're making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, 'I notice it's more expensive than last year,' it's, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I've paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’"
Costagli noted that small bags were the only package size seeing sales growth through mid-October, while large and extra-large sizes experienced the sharpest declines.
U.S. candy prices have outpaced general inflation for several years.
Government data shows candy and gum prices jumped 44% over a five-year period through September, while overall grocery costs rose 22.5% over the same timeframe.
Discount grocer Aldi advertised a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolates—including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers—for $19.87 this week.
That is nearly the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece pack five years ago.
High cocoa prices are the primary driver. Global cocoa costs hit a record $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 due to harsh weather in West Africa, which produces 70% of world supply, and speculative futures trading, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Although cocoa dropped to $3,241 per metric ton in March, prices rebounded in the spring after the Iran war disrupted fertilizer shipments to Africa.
The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to dampen output, bringing heat and dry conditions through February.
Costagli noted that demand remains weak even where prices have dropped. Non-chocolate treats like gummies and lollipops averaged $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, down roughly 3% from last year, without driving a surge in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser at Circana, said consumers are coping with high grocery bills by making smaller, more frequent shopping trips right before using items.
She questioned whether buyers are simply holding off until closer to Halloween.
"People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general," she said. "I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed."
The National Confectioners Association, representing producers such as Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic.
"We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong," the group said Friday in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
articles.title_zh: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
articles.content_orig:
JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.
You check your credit score, see nothing unusual and assume your identity is safe. But what if someone has already stolen your personal information and your credit report shows absolutely nothing? That's entirely possible.
Credit monitoring can help detect certain types of identity theft, particularly fraud involving new credit accounts. However, criminals can also target your existing bank accounts, retirement savings, government benefits and phone number without triggering a traditional credit alert. As a result, a clean credit report can give you a false sense of security. Here's what credit monitoring can catch, what it might miss and how to better protect yourself.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money
In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
IDENTITY THEFT PROTECTION IS CHANGING: WHAT TO LOOK FOR
Reviewing financial statements regularly can help uncover suspicious activity that may never appear on your credit report. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Credit monitoring tracks changes to your credit file. Depending on the service, it can alert you to suspicious activity involving your credit history.
These alerts can help you discover new account fraud before the damage grows. However, credit monitoring depends on information that lenders and other companies report to credit bureaus. Therefore, it cannot reliably detect identity theft that occurs entirely outside the credit reporting system.
Criminals have several ways to misuse your information, steal money or make you more vulnerable to fraud without triggering a traditional credit monitoring alert. Here are six situations worth watching for.
A criminal gains access to your existing checking account, savings account, retirement account or payment app. Because the account already exists, the takeover may never appear on your credit report. Instead, you might first discover the theft through an unfamiliar transaction or a notification from your financial institution.
Someone uses your Social Security number to file a fraudulent tax return or claim government benefits. You may receive an IRS notice about a tax return you never filed. Alternatively, you could discover unemployment benefits claimed in your name. Neither situation necessarily changes your credit score.
A thief uses your health insurance information to receive medical care, prescriptions or equipment. You might then receive bills for services you never used. Even worse, someone else's medical information could end up in your records. Traditional credit monitoring generally will not detect the misuse itself, although unpaid debts could eventually create other financial complications.
Criminals may convince your mobile carrier to transfer your phone number to a SIM card or device they control. Once they have your number, they may intercept certain verification codes and attempt to access your accounts. A sudden loss of cellular service could be an early warning sign, especially if you did not request a change.
A scammer tricks you into authorizing a wire transfer, sending money through a payment app or purchasing gift cards. Because you initiated the payment, even under false pretenses, traditional credit monitoring may have no indication that anything happened. Your financial institution might have separate fraud detection systems, but those protections vary.
Your name, phone number, address and other personal details may appear on people-search websites or data broker databases. Criminals can use that information to create convincing phishing messages or impersonation scams. Although the exposure itself does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity, it can make you a more attractive target. The Federal Trade Commission identifies unauthorized bank withdrawals, unfamiliar medical bills and fraudulent tax filings among the warning signs of identity theft.
SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW
Criminals can access existing financial accounts or misuse payment information without triggering traditional credit monitoring alerts. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A credit score provides a snapshot of your creditworthiness based on information in your credit file. It does not show every account you own, or every place someone might use your personal information. For example, someone could access your retirement account while your credit score remains unchanged.
Similarly, criminals might use your phone number to get into an existing account without ever applying for credit. That's why it's important to review your actual credit reports rather than relying on your score alone. Even then, you'll need to check your other accounts separately.
Fortunately, you can look for suspicious activity without paying for an expensive monitoring service. Start with these six habits.
Check your bank statements, investment accounts, retirement accounts and payment apps for unfamiliar transactions. Also, enable transaction and security alerts whenever your financial institutions offer them.
Pay attention to IRS notices about returns you did not file or income from employers you don't recognize. You can also review your federal tax account through the official IRS website at irs.gov/ . You can also request a free six-digit Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) from the IRS. This helps prevent someone else from filing a fraudulent federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new IP PIN each year.
Review your earnings history periodically to see whether it matches your actual employment. You can access your information through your my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Unexpected earnings may require further investigation.
Look for unfamiliar medical appointments, prescriptions, procedures or insurance claims. If something looks suspicious, contact your health insurance company or medical provider directly.
Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM swap safeguards. Additionally, consider using an authenticator app or security key instead of text-message verification when available.
Search for your name, phone number and address to identify information exposed through people-search websites. You can request removal from individual sites or consider a reputable data removal service.
Pro tip: Choose one day each month to review your accounts and important records. You can combine it with a bill-payment routine to make the habit easier to maintain.
Monitoring your online accounts and enabling security alerts can help you spot potential identity theft before the damage grows. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Credit monitoring remains useful, but it cannot catch every type of identity theft. Some identity theft protection services offer broader monitoring that can help identify suspicious activity involving financial accounts, personal information and online accounts. However, the features and level of protection depend on the provider and plan you choose.
Before signing up, compare the features, coverage limits and costs. Pay attention to which financial accounts qualify for monitoring and whether the service offers restoration assistance if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike Russian targets 2,500 kilometers from border
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike Russian targets 2,500 kilometers from border
articles.content_orig:
Help us keep bringing the truth to light, even when Russia turns the lights out.
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border on Oct. 24, monitoring channels reported.
A fire first broke out at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
The facility is one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, and the company behind Omsky Kauchuk says the site is a leading producer of synthetic rubber, organic synthesis products, and methyl tert-butyl ether, an additive used to refine gasoline.
The plant is part of Russia's supply chain for rocket fuel, including for the Iskander ballistic missile used in fatal attacks against Ukraine, Exilenova Plus said.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25. At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22.
Later, a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Ozon was also hit in the Ukrainian drone attack, Exilenova Plus reported .
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaliy Khotsenko confirmed that the region was targeted by Ukrainian drones, saying that a logistics hub in the city of Omsk was hit.
"A logistics hub in Omsk was attacked by a drone. Personnel were promptly evacuated. Emergency services are working at the scene," he claimed.
Reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Ozon and its competitor Wildberries have been targeted by Ukrainian forces in recent months. The two are a major part of Russia's economy, with their broader ecosystems accounting for about 8.5% of Russia's GDP.
Ukraine has targeted facilities that often serve as storage sites for dual-use goods used in weapons production and other military purposes.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Omsk Oblast was also under fire in an attack on Oct. 8. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck the Omsk oil refinery .
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," Ukraine's General Staff said .
More recently, on Oct. 24, the General Staff said that Ukrainian forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, as well as an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai.
The synthetic rubbers are used to make solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.
"Damage to such objects affects the supply chain of raw materials for the Russian missile program," Ukraine's General Staff wrote.
Volodymyr Ivanyshyn is a news editor for The Kyiv Independent. He is pursuing an Honors Bachelor of Arts at the University of Toronto, majoring in political science with a minor in anthropology and human geography. Volodymyr holds a Certificate in Business Fundamentals from Rotman Commerce at the University of Toronto. He previously completed an internship with The Kyiv Independent.
MegaGRINN is the largest shopping complex in Belgorod, covering over 163,000 square meters and housing more than 200 shops. The center was closed and empty of visitors during the reported overnight attack.
The gas project was part of an energy deal discussed by U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during their September visit to the Kremlin, sources told the New York Times.

articles.title_orig: Three days before election, Netanyahu warns Iran is preparing to destroy Israel
articles.title_zh: Three days before election, Netanyahu warns Iran is preparing to destroy Israel
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Israelis are protesting against the government and calling for an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks .
Demonstrators rallied in the public plaza known as Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday, three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
Elsewhere in Israel, protesters were also gathering for antigovernment demonstrations, reported Haaretz newspaper.
Taking part were leading figures from opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main centre-right rival.
In Tel Aviv, Eisenkot was greeted by chants of “Who’s coming? The next prime minister”, according to The Times of Israel. The leader of the Democrats, Yair Golan, was also at the rally.
“Masses, masses of masses, flowing in the ‘Democrats’ march from Rabin Square to the Hostages Square – for change, for hope, for r-e-v-o-l-u-t-i-o-n. What energy. This time it’s ours completely!”, Israeli citizen and lawyer Dan Adin posted on X.
Polls ahead of Tuesday’s election suggest a tight race, with Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, in power since late 2022, neck and neck with Eisenkot’s. Neither bloc is currently projected to obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s parliament.
The election could be pivotal in determining whether Israel launches another round of strikes on Iran. Eisenkot is believed to be less inclined to resume military action against Tehran if he becomes Israel’s next prime minister.
However, on most other foreign policy issues, leading Israeli parties and politicians remain united, including in their opposition to the creation of an independent Palestinian state.
Ahead of the protest, the October Council alerted law enforcement to possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
“We have sent an urgent letter to the Police Commissioner following alerts about attempts by entities linked to the coalition to disrupt tonight’s rally,” it wrote on X.
The October Council aims to hold Israeli officials deemed responsible for the October 7 attacks to account and deliver justice for affected families.
Netanyahu’s coalition government, however, has refused demands to establish an independent commission of inquiry. Instead, it has offered to set up a “political” commission. Half of the commission’s members would be appointed by the government, while the remainder would be appointed by opposition legislators.
Opposition leaders have said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

articles.title_orig: Six Flags adding seat belts to Goliath rollercoaster following death
articles.title_zh: Six Flags adding seat belts to Goliath rollercoaster following death
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags has announced it will be adding seat belts to some of its rollercoasters after a man fell to his death on the Goliath ride in the US state of Georgia earlier this month.
The company's CEO John Reilly said in a letter to customers late on Friday that the company is reinforcing safety measure across its parks, including adding seat belts to Goliath and similar rides, which already feature lap bar restraints.
The chain of amusement parks has 34 locations across North America, with over 220 rollercoasters in total.
Georgia's Goliath ride will remain closed pending safety reviews and out of an abundance of caution, so will eight other rides at five other parks, Reilly added.
The CEO also said the company has hired independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across all its amusement parks. The company is committed to taking action based on the experts' findings and will share progress updates, he said.
On 12 October, a 42-year-old man named Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed at Six Flags Over Georgia after being ejected from the Goliath, police have said. Four other passengers were injured as he fell.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"Our hearts remain with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, those injured, and everyone impacted by the tragic incident," Reilly said in his letter.
"What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags," he added.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five
Over 28 million guests visit Six Flags locations every year, according to the company's website.
October's fatal incident was not the first time a passenger has been hurt at one of the parks.
An Iraq War veteran died in 2011 after being ejected from a ride in New York. In 2013, a woman died after slipping from her restraints and falling 75 feet from a coaster in Texas.
In 2022, a 22-year-old man died from a brain injury after riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California. His family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.
The following month, the California park announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride .
