articles.title_orig: The Rare-Earth Vultures Harvesting Metals From America’s Old Wind Turbines
articles.title_zh: The Rare-Earth Vultures Harvesting Metals From America’s Old Wind Turbines
articles.content_orig:
The technologies transforming modern industry depend on materials that rarely receive the same attention as the innovations they make possible. Artificial intelligence, robotics, electric vehicles, advanced aerospace systems, and high-performance electronics all rely on sophisticated components whose production requires access to specialized minerals.
Perhaps the most strategically important are rare earth elements, particularly those used in high-performance permanent magnets. And while the technology industry continues pushing the boundaries of what machines can accomplish, another challenge is gaining urgency: finding dependable new sources of the materials needed to manufacture them.
China dominates much of the world’s rare earth processing and magnet production, creating a concentrated supply chain that governments and manufacturers are increasingly determined to diversify.
That effort is directing attention toward resource-rich countries such as Brazil. But discovering new mineral deposits is only part of the solution.
The next important technological advances may come from finding better ways to recover the minerals already being discovered.
Why Rare Earth Recovery Technology Matters
Rare earth elements aren’t necessarily rare in Earth’s crust. The difficulty often lies in identifying deposits with useful concentrations of valuable elements and developing efficient methods to separate and recover them.
Terbium and dysprosium illustrate the challenge. These heavy rare earth elements help certain permanent magnets retain their strength at elevated temperatures, making them valuable in electric vehicle motors, industrial robotics, wind turbines, and aerospace equipment.
For manufacturers, access to these materials is closely connected to product performance and supply reliability. For companies developing new mineral resources, the question becomes how to extract them in ways that are technically practical, environmentally manageable, and potentially commercially viable.
One area attracting attention is ionic adsorption clay, a type of rare earth-bearing deposit in which certain elements can be recovered through chemical leaching.
Unlike conventional hard-rock mining, some ionic clay deposits may offer opportunities to investigate alternative extraction approaches, potentially reducing the amount of material that must be excavated and processed.
And in Brazil, researchers are exploring what those possibilities could mean for future rare earth supplies.
A Brazilian Project Combining Scale With Technical Progress
Among the companies investigating these opportunities is IMC Rare Earths Ltd. (NYSE American: IMC), which is advancing its Itarantim rare earth project across portions of Bahia and Minas Gerais.
Itarantim hosts a reported 1.1-billion-tonne inferred mineral resource containing the four principal magnet rare earth elements: neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
That geological scale provides a strong foundation for exploration, but it’s the company’s recent metallurgical testing that adds another dimension to the project.
In September, laboratory work conducted with Brazil’s IFRN and CT Mineral reported terbium recovery reaching 95.2% in the best-performing test , with an average recovery of 81.1% in the reported composite. The company also produced a mixed rare earth carbonate, an intermediate material that can be further processed into separated rare earth products.
Separate research at the University of Brighton in the United Kingdom recovered 73% of the total rare earth elements tested, excluding cerium, using an acidified magnesium sulfate solution. The same testing recovered 71.4% of terbium and 70.5% of dysprosium.
These results were obtained under different laboratory conditions and should not be treated as interchangeable recovery rates. Nevertheless, they show how Itarantim’s mineralization responds to potential extraction methods.
And that information is central to evaluating what comes next.
Could Rare Earths Be Recovered Through Wells?
One of the more intriguing possibilities emerging from testing is in-situ recovery .
Rather than excavating large volumes of rare earth-bearing clay, the proposed method involves injecting a suitable solution through injection wells, letting it interact with the mineralized material, and recovering the resulting rare earth-bearing liquid through extraction wells.
The minerals would then undergo further processing to produce intermediate materials suitable for eventual refining.
If successfully demonstrated under field conditions, this approach could potentially reduce excavation, material transportation, and the need for extensive tailings storage. It might also offer advantages in surface disturbance and infrastructure requirements compared with certain conventional mining methods.
The technology is not yet commercially validated at Itarantim. Field testing must establish whether fluids can move effectively through the deposit, remain controlled, and be recovered reliably.
But the laboratory findings provide a reason to investigate those possibilities further.
Another encouraging observation concerns the composition of the recovered solutions. In the University of Brighton tests, uranium and thorium remained below detection limits in the leachate. IMC has also reported negligible deleterious elements in certain tested solutions.
These results do not establish that the entire deposit is free of radioactivity. They do, however, provide potentially useful information for researchers, regulators, and development partners assessing processing requirements, environmental considerations, and future waste management.
As the technology becomes increasingly focused on efficiency and resource management, those characteristics could become important as testing advances.
New Discoveries Expand the Scientific Questions
While the metallurgical work continues, IMC is also investigating mineralization beyond its existing resource boundaries.
On October 8, the company announced a new high-grade, terbium-rich zone at Block H, where drilling identified seven meters of mineralization beginning just two meters below the surface, including a higher-grade three-meter section.
Preliminary testing recovered 64% to 83% of terbium from samples taken from the upper portion of the enriched zone.
The discovery lies outside Itarantim’s currently defined resource, creating another area for exploration. At Block D, drilling has also identified 20 meters of continuous mineralization, with additional work planned to investigate its extent.
Together, these findings are helping researchers examine both the deposit’s geological characteristics and recovery methods suitable for different mineralized areas.
IMC has engaged ANSTO Minerals in Australia for further metallurgical studies and is evaluating potential processing approaches, including in-situ, vat, and heap leaching.
Next stages will include additional resource definition, engineering evaluation, field testing, and potential partnerships with industrial and government organizations that can support future development.
The Technology Behind a More Diversified Supply Chain
The global effort to diversify rare earth supplies is often discussed in terms of geopolitics and mineral discoveries. Yet processing technology may prove equally important.
A large mineral resource cannot contribute to manufacturing supply chains unless its valuable elements can be recovered, refined, and delivered in forms that industry can use.
That makes the work taking place at projects such as Itarantim relevant beyond the mining sector. Laboratory research, chemical processing, geological modeling, and engineering innovation all support efforts to establish new sources of materials essential to advanced technology.
Brazil’s substantial rare earth potential offers opportunities to continue that work, while international cooperation could connect emerging mineral projects with the processing

articles.title_orig: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA: "Now is the time"
articles.title_zh: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with CIA: "Now is the time"
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Cubans seeking "positive change" to work with the CIA, the latest ploy in the growing efforts from the Trump administration to remove Cuba's communist regime from power.
"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio wrote Friday on X. "The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."
Shortly afterward, the CIA reposted Rubio's message and a similar call in Spanish for Cubans to work with the agency. A video was posted alongside the message showing the steps needed to contact the intelligence agency.
A strict U.S. embargo and sanctions seeking to put pressure on Cuba's communist government have led to prices of basic goods skyrocketing and decreased access to medical care for its citizens. Cubans reported waiting in bread lines for hours and others reported lining up to see a doctor.
Last week, the U.S. government announced additional economic sanctions on Cuba's state-run bank, saying the institution had ties to Iran.
President Trump said on Friday during a campaign rally in South Florida that "we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran." He was referring to the U.S. Navy warships deployed near the Strait of Hormuz.
Mr. Trump added: "Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."
Cuba's government has pushed back, with Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla responding Friday on X , saying: "We reject any threats stemming from U.S. ambitions toward Cuba."
Rodriguez Parrilla added: "Our shores are lined with beautiful beaches, but they are also rugged and inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile intentions and a desire for domination."
Olivia  Gazis contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: AI tool REA cracks paid software: Is the software industry's business model coming to an end?
articles.title_zh: AI tool REA cracks paid software: Is the software industry's business model coming to an end?
articles.content_orig:
It was predicted, just in a slightly different way: rather than having to buy software in the long run, you'd simply have your AI agents program the features you need. Now there's another development: take an expensive paid app on your PC, run REA on it, and your AI can learn the professional tool's entire codebase and functionality before rebuilding it as open-source software.
A few days ago, we reported on programmer and entrepreneur Brandon Thomas, who, frustrated with Adobe, decided to recreate almost the entire Adobe suite as open-source software under the project name ArtCraft, making it freely available to everyone. This includes Premiere, After Effects, and more. Thomas has years of programming experience, but what if anyone could do this soon?
That's where the new open-source tool REA comes in. The acronym stands for Reverse Engineer Anything. REA connects AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
REA analyzes software based on instructions given in natural language to understand how it works, even when the original source code isn't available. While REA can't always recover the original source code exactly, it can reconstruct readable code based on the software's functionality. This reconstruction gives an AI agent enough information to replicate parts of the software, ideally achieving comparable results with newly written code. The result is a custom implementation that delivers the same functionality.
Using a new codebase for the implementation could also make copyright enforcement more difficult in practice, since the original source code hasn't actually been stolen. And that's precisely where the potential for market disruption lies. Functionally recreating software is legally different from copying its protected source code.
REA significantly lowers the barrier to entry, and this app is almost certainly just the beginning. Instead of having to understand everything yourself, you can ask the AI questions and give it tasks in natural language. However, a fair amount of technical knowledge is still required for now, including installation, working with the tools, and verifying the results. That said, YouTube and other platforms promise easy-to-follow tutorials that can help users get around some of these hurdles.
More accessible reverse engineering could mark a major technological leap. Recreating software is becoming cheaper. But that doesn't automatically mean smaller players will necessarily benefit. At the same time, competition could intensify, shifting the focus away from features and exclusive code toward usability, reliability, data, ecosystems, customer support, trust, and ongoing development. This is where large corporations have an advantage, potentially putting even more pressure on smaller developers.
I didn't try REA with the powerful Claude Code because it's too expensive for me. Instead, I'm using the ad-supported, free app Freebuff (don't provide sensible data!).
I instructed the AI to install REA and all its dependencies, along with MCP and Ghidra. From there, the entire process ran automatically, and I didn't have to do anything else.
Next, I wanted to recreate an app. It shouldn't be as complicated as a game, but not as simple as a calculator either. The VLC Media Player came to mind, so I entered the following prompt:
The agent got to work, asked me three more questions, and finished after about 10 to 15 minutes. I had my own VLC clone. I was also informed that it used Chromium rather than libVLC as its engine, meaning some video formats wouldn't work. That could be changed, though.
The “Own Player” worked right from the start. I simply dragged an MP3 file into the window, and playback began immediately. I could also open folders, although subfolders weren't included. Keyboard shortcuts for seeking, muting, and other functions worked perfectly. The only issue was that fullscreen mode displayed a black screen.
Overall, though, the result was impressive for just a few minutes of work. Once everything was installed, virtually all it took to create an app was a single prompt and answers to three multiple-choice questions.
Reverse engineering is nothing new. But AI is lowering the barriers to entry and making the process increasingly straightforward, even for non-coders. And that's precisely what could put software copyright law to the test: if anyone can easily recreate their own apps from paid software, this could threaten software vendors' business models.
Not every copy is legal, of course, but under certain conditions, functionality can be recreated without using the original code. As a result, the code that software vendors spent so much money developing could lose some of its value as a competitive advantage, even if their copyrights remain untouched. This could reshape the software market in the long term, potentially in disruptive ways.
In the past, you bought software and owned a copy. Then came the subscription era, when software was licensed for use rather than sold outright. If everyone can build their own apps—or recreate existing ones—the software licensing model will likely be affected as well.

articles.title_zh: New ‘Mass Effect 5’ Details Emerge After Cancellation, And It Sounds Great
articles.content_orig:
Avi Lewis, leader of one of Canada's top opposition parties, wants the Canadian government to help save Mass Effect developer BioWare. The leader of the New Democratic Party took to social media to speak out against publisher EA.
On October 21, EA announced a major shift in strategy and a significant internal restructuring that involves the cancellation of a number of projects, the closure of BioWare in Edmonton , and a reported 400 people losing their jobs. The studio, known for franchises like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, was shut down after more than 30 years of creating beloved role-playing games. It reportedly had 50 people working on the next Mass Effect, all of which were cut.
Lewis linked BioWare's closure to the $55 billion EA acquisition by an investor group composed of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners, approved in December 2025. Since the acquisition, EA has been focusing only on its biggest brands — Battlefield and its sports titles, predominantly — while other series have been pushed aside.
"This is private equity, this is what it does. Buy up businesses, run them into the ground, and rip them apart for short-term profit," Lewis wrote on X / Twitter .
"The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity — and the federal support — to buy it and run it themselves. And if we want to avoid the Mass Effect effect in Canada, we should be keeping private equity out, not welcoming it in."
It's not a huge surprise that a Canadian official would be plugged into the games industry. Canada already offers significant federal and provincial tax relief to support video game development studios, offsetting costs, which is why so many studios set up a permanent base in major Canadian cities. It's a government that's traditionally understood the value gaming brings to a modern economy.
One question fans have is whether or not EA might be willing to sell off BioWare franchises such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age to another studio. IGN spoke to a number of video game industry analysts to find out whether that was likely, and why EA decided to close BioWare down .
A day after EA's announcement, a trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online . It showed alien smooching, blue tentacle-headed women, and included a title for the game: Mass Effect Universe.
BioWare was a hugely influential studio and basically invented RPG conversation wheels, which have become standard in the genre. Upcoming games The Expanse: Osiris Reborn and Exodus both owe a lot to Mass Effect .

Jessica Vuittonet says her brother, who does not have a criminal record, has been detained by ICE.
Vuittonet says her brother is among those arrested by Trumpâs immigration goons. She says she voted for Trump for religious reasons, but now realizes Trumpâs policies are âheartbreaking.â
âItâs hardworking men that are being detained by ICE, not criminals,â she said. âThat are up in the roofs, that are doing somebodyâs driveway, that are cutting somebodyâs grass, that are literally having a work truck to go work. Where are the criminals you said you were going to arrest? Yes, thereâs a few that youâve done, but the majority have been hardworking people.â
She continued, âHardworking women. I just want to tear upâwomen that Iâve seen with their children, walking every day to school. Whereâs your mom? Kids staying behindâbroken families, it is just heartbreaking.â
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Trumpâs violent crackdown, which has reportedly led to around 980,000 people being deported , most of whom have no criminal record, has sparked regret among many Trump voters who wanted to see criminals removed from the countryânot innocent families violently split apart.
Benny Melendez, who has installed fences on construction sites he manages to protect his workers from ICE, says he also regrets voting for Trumpâjust as he regretted voting for Biden in 2020.
Melendez tells CBS News that so many arrests in his Texas community have made it hard to find workers, and building a house can take twice as long because of a lack of manpower. According to TRAC , Texas, a state that has voted for Trump in all three of his presidential elections, has more immigration detentions than any other state.
Trumpâs approval rating has fallen to a record low of 32 percent, according to CNN , just weeks ahead of the midterms that are expected to be a bloodbath for Republicans, who are at serious risk of losing their majorities in both the House and Senate.
The economy has proven to be the most stubborn issue for most Americans, with two-thirds of voters, and one-third of Republicans , saying the president has made economic conditions worse.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stands with White House Border Czar Tom Homan, and Attorney General Pam Bondi before former U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin is sworn in as the next secretary of the Department of Homeland Security in the Oval Office at the White House on March 24, 2026.
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
While polling has suggested that immigration is unlikely to be a definitional issue ahead of Novemberâs elections, Michigan State University political scientist Matthew Grossman told The Guardian that Trumpâs deportation policies were part of a general feeling of the president having â gone too far ,â a sentiment also seen in terms of the Iran war and tariffs .
However, the issue hasnât fazed White House border czar Tom Homan: âMy job as a border czar is to keep that border secure and enforce immigration law,â he told CBS News earlier this month. âI particularly donât care about midterms.â

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo looks better out of the box but apparently soon falls behind Galaxy Z Fold 8 in what matters most to me
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo looks better out of the box but apparently soon falls behind Galaxy Z Fold 8 in what matters most to me
articles.content_orig:
Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo . Analysts have speculated that Samsung’s Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that.
In a new blog post , Samsung UK crows that the company’s 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year’s models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn’t talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention.
The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn’t release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn’t mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent.
Samsung noted last month that US preorders for the Galaxy Z8 series were trending 30 percent higher than last year, but it hasn’t confirmed any updated numbers for the US market. This meshes with third-party reports, which claimed Samsung was ramping up foldable manufacturing, particularly of the wider, iPhone-like Z Fold 8. The company isn’t talking about the proportion of Z Fold 8 versus Z Fold 8 Ultra sales, but it seems likely that Samsung’s wider foldable is doing better in the wake of Apple’s foldable announcement.
Samsung released its first foldable phone in 2019, and it was the only company seriously pursuing the form factor for several years. Those early devices were clunky and more interesting as feats of engineering than as things you’d want to carry around all day, but little by little, foldable hardware improved until Apple could finally release the product it wanted. The iPhone Duo is not an island—it relies on many of the same components as other foldable phones, including Samsung displays.
The Apple hype train is unstoppable, so increased interest in foldables was probably inevitable. Samsung expanded its foldable lineup with the non-Ultra model just in time, likely based on leaks of Apple’s device. But the wider form factor isn’t just a gimmick—it addresses several annoying issues with foldable phones. The main display is better for watching video with less wasted space. It’s also better for reading documents and using unoptimized apps (many of which are in the Play Store) in portrait orientation compared to square foldable screens. This is a positive change for foldable phones, and one we’ll probably see replicated by other OEMs in the coming months.
Regardless, foldable pricing is definitely not cool. It’s hard to justify spending $2,000 on a phone, but at the same time, all devices are getting more expensive. With recent price hikes, the top-end flat phones from Samsung, Google, and Apple are only a few hundred dollars away from their foldable options. Foldable prices have inched upward, too, but not by the same amount. Apple even managed an uncharacteristically competitive (for a foldable) price of $2,000 for the iPhone Duo. Samsung’s wide foldable is a little cheaper at $1,900, and it has been discounted at a few retailers since launch.

articles.title_orig: Gamers are now playing Steam games directly on PlayStation 5, no streaming required
articles.title_zh: Gamers are now playing Steam games directly on PlayStation 5, no streaming required
articles.content_orig:
PlayStation 5 owners are beginning to run Windows PC games from their Steam libraries directly on jailbroken consoles. Unlike Remote Play or cloud gaming, the games are executed locally using the PS5 hardware. Several projects now support this functionality, although game compatibility and performance remain limited.
One recent demonstration comes from X user ‘v7dt1’, who shared footage of a Steam booting into UI on his PlayStation 5. He explained that the game was downloaded from Steam and executed directly on the console. However, he also admitted that the game eventually crashed and that getting everything to work remains difficult. The exact software used in his demonstration has not been confirmed. It appears that this user is using something called Playden for PS5.
One of the projects making this possible is Playden for PS5 . First made publicly available earlier this month, Playden allows users to sign in to Steam, browse their libraries, download games and launch them directly from the PS5 home screen. It uses prospero-win, a port of Wine for PlayStation 5, rather than requiring a separate Linux installation.
The software supports Direct3D 8 through 11 using DXVK, while Direct3D 12 games use VKD3D-Proton. According to the project’s compatibility database, games such as Cyberpunk 2077, Hollow Knight, Cuphead, Portal 2, Dead Cells and Deep Rock Galactic have reached playable states. Cyberpunk 2077 was tested for 13 minutes with a controller, although no frame rate measurements were provided. These results should not be interpreted as confirmation that the games work without problems.
Playden has already received several updates, with version 0.6.0 arriving this week. The latest update adds support for importing Windows games from USB storage or FTP, 120 Hz output and additional display settings. However, online multiplayer remains unsupported, and games requiring third-party launchers or certain anti-cheat systems cannot run.
Here’s an actual demo featuring Potal on PlayStation through Playden:
Testing Steam games on Playden! by u/Cevap in PS5_Jailbreak
Worth adding that this is not Steam running inside Linux on PS5. There is no need to boot into Linux, as Playden runs as a native PS5 application accessible from the console’s home screen. However, multiplayer games are not currently supported, and users should be cautious about connecting their Steam accounts to experimental software. Also, this should be obvious, but Playden requires a jailbroken PS5.
Source: Playden for PS5 (Github) , Compatibility list

articles.title_orig: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
articles.title_zh: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
articles.content_orig:
A drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca , a study found.
Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.
The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.
That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed.
"I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.
The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility."
The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.
Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.
Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.
He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years.
Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.
Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone.
Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.
Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it.
Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer.
Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.
The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches.
Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own.
She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread.
In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since.
"I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

articles.title_orig: Swap The Bathtub Curtain: Add Privacy With An Amazon Alternative
articles.title_zh: Swap The Bathtub Curtain: Add Privacy With An Amazon Alternative
articles.content_orig:
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Shower curtains are a solid option for many bathrooms, but they aren't always the best choice. In the wrong room, they can make the space feel small, get in the way while you're cleaning, or become pretty gross. If you're tired of clingy fabric, but still need a little privacy, the Frosted Bathtub Shower Door by EGrinbey on Amazon is a potential swap for a shower curtain , with the frost adding a layer of protection compared to clear ones.
This product is minimal enough that you can easily fit it in most bathrooms. It features lightly frosted glass and sleek, black hardware for something simple and elegant. According to the Amazon page, the door should work for any opening measuring 56-60 inches wide and 60 inches tall. However, the seller does note that the lower slider is 1.9 inches wide. Whatever you are installing the door on top of, you have to make sure it is wider than that for it to fit properly.
Cost is one of the important things to consider before installing a new shower door . Thankfully, while it is certainly expensive compared to a cheap plastic film, it is under $400, which is a steal compared to having a professional do the work. "Awesome shower door for the money," said a 5-star reviewer on Amazon .
This shower door is relatively easy to install, even for a beginner. However, you do have to cut and drill in the right spots to get everything in the correct placement and prevent leaks. When cutting, measure the total length for your shower space and the metal carefully. The same goes for marking where you need to drill holes; double-check that everything is in the right position before you mark anything. It's always a good idea to read through the instructions in preparation for starting a project, but especially in this case, as a mistake could make the whole door impossible to use for your bathroom.
Patience is also key. As you install this product, you want to be careful not to damage the doors in any way. There is something known as the exploding glass shower door phenomenon . Though this is SGCC-certified tempered — which means it is more likely to just crack or shatter into safe pieces – you still don't want to risk it cracking or exploding.
The other thing you need to check before you start installing your doors is that you are setting them up the right way. For this particular product, only one side slides. It's easy to flip it either way, but you have to set it up correctly to suit your needs, or you may be stuck trying to squeeze between your toilet and tub every time you need to shower.
There is also occasionally the issue of the shower door not fitting, despite the given measurements being perfect for your space. Some reviews mention that the details provided on the product page aren't exactly accurate. "Defective shower door. One side of the glass was too short and water was spilling out," said a 1-star review on Amazon .
It's not uncommon to buy an item when it goes on sale, or you have the money, and then open it to install it months later. However, It's a good idea to check that everything is included, and that the measurements are correct as soon as you get it. That way, you have time to return it through Amazon before the period ends. It's a bit of a pain, especially if you need to put it away again until you're ready to install, but it can save you a lot of frustration later.
Shower doors must fit your space very closely, so that you don't have to deal with gaps or leaks. Some reviewers mention measuring the length and width of all pieces several times, just to make sure everything will fit properly. You may also want to check the measurements in different spots, for both your door and the place you are installing it, as rooms aren't always even, either. What may seem like the right length in one spot may end up being too short in another.

articles.title_orig: 'The transit world is where innovation goes to die' — The U.S. lags far behind on using driverless trains, but new projects could open the floodgates
articles.title_zh: 'The transit world is where innovation goes to die' — The U.S. lags far behind on using driverless trains, but new projects could open the floodgates
articles.content_orig:
Even as automated vehicles such as robotaxis grow more prevalent in the U.S., almost every mass transit system still requires a driver or operator on board. Two major cities are seeking to change that.
Officials in Washington, D.C., recently advanced a plan that could let computers fully control one of its subways, and Los Angeles is seeking to build a new, completely automated line. Honolulu already has one.
The Washington and LA projects, which would take years to implement and still face financial and technical hurdles, come amid an already fierce debate over the safety risks and benefits of automated trains and whether the substantial upfront expense is worth the long-term savings in labor costs.
Supporters call the push long overdue, pointing out that American cities lag far behind numerous places across the world that run unattended subways, metros or buses, including several cities in Europe and Asia, as well as major systems in Canada, Australia, South America and the Middle East.
“It should be much harder to automate something that’s on-road, that has all of these various obstacles coming at it, compared to a fixed-rail system,” said Baruch Feigenbaum, senior managing director of transportation policy at the Reason Foundation, a libertarian think tank that has advocated for transit automation. “I don’t know a nice way to say this, but basically the transit world is where innovation goes to die.”
Only in recent years have on-road vehicles from such companies as Waymo, Tesla and Zoox taken the automation lead in the U.S. ahead of transit systems using a track. In fact, although operators have always been part of the Metro subway system in Washington, D.C., trains ran with some automated features when it opened 50 years ago. After a 2009 fatal crash, those were turned off, then restored over the past two years.
Now, officials in the nation’s capital have renewed their push for automation on Metro’s Red Line. And an environmental review is underway in Los Angeles for an automated track for a new underground line of its heavy-rail system that would cut through the rough terrain of the Santa Monica Mountains.
Honolulu is already running an elevated driverless line — the most expansive automated transit system in the U.S. It’ll stretch 19 miles when completed, surpassing the elevated driverless trains Detroit and Miami opened as pilot projects in the 1980s, a monorail connecting hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and smaller systems that carry passengers between airport terminals.
An automated monorail that once ran in Memphis, Tennessee, closed down years ago. And the driverless Jacksonville Skyway will indefinitely halt operations soon due to budget cuts, despite initial plans for an even larger automated system.
After nine people were killed and many others injured in the 2009 train collision near the Fort Totten station on the D.C. Red Line, the National Transportation Safety Board blamed the crash on a maintenance problem in the automated signaling system that separates trains from one another.
Randy Clarke, CEO of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority , pointed out in an interview with The Associated Press that the issue in Fort Totten had nothing to do with the cruise control-like system that was restored on the Red Line in 2024 and the other Metro lines last year. Still, he acknowledged that for many years the crash “paralyzed” Metro’s plans for further automation.
“That was a big failure, there’s no question. We do not do anything like that now,” said Clarke, who called the current system “highly regulated, highly documented, very proficient.”
Trains could conceivably run without a human worker inside the cab as early as 2033 under the nearly $1 billion plan Metro’s Board of Directors backed in April to upgrade the Red Line with safety features including protective barriers that prevent passengers from getting onto the tracks.
Clarke said that even if workers aren’t needed to physically run the trains, they will be needed to maintain the tracks and respond to emergencies.
Unions have been critics of automation. John Samuelsen, a former worker in the New York subway system who now serves as international president of the Transport Workers Union, said unions have fought off automation efforts in New York and elsewhere, calling them “a catastrophe waiting to happen.”
“Passengers will be left dealing with a self-evacuation, which is a disaster in a system which runs on a third rail,” Samuelsen said.
To alleviate massive traffic bottlenecks for commuters, Honolulu opened its Skyline automated light metro transit system three years ago and expanded it last year.
Vance Tsuda, the system’s project director, said there hasn’t been a single crash or injury associated with automation. Even hybrid systems are less safe than a completely automated one, he said, arguing that a human is far more likely to overlook something like an open door and prematurely clear a train for departure.
“If you have somebody making that decision, they could make a wrong decision,” Tsuda said.
But David King, an associate professor of urban planning at Arizona State University who has researched automated transportation, said the success rate has to remain perfect to keep the public trust. That’s why the Fort Totten crash and others involving automation put the technology so far behind, he said.
“We allow a certain amount of failure with private industry that we don’t tolerate when the state does it,” said King, citing the several rockets blown up by Elon Musk’s SpaceX — a record he argues would cripple NASA’s budget if it happened in the public sector.
Perhaps the most ambitious transit automation effort being pursued in the U.S. is the subway line Los Angeles officials voted to recommend beneath the Santa Monica Mountains. The area is one of the most notorious traffic headaches in the country, with the mountains dividing the bustling Westside employment hub from the San Fernando Valley.
There’s already a subway system under the same mountain range near Hollywood, but that one has a driver onboard. The new proposal, which is undergoing an environmental review, would use shorter, more frequent trains, said Cecily Way, who oversees planning for the Sepulveda Project for LA Metro.
Like the project in Washington, the new line in Los Angeles would feature station doors to protect passengers on the platform from oncoming trains.
Feigenbaum with the Reason Foundation said that automation of a major transit line such as in Los Angeles or Washington could open the floodgates for other cities to follow.
“It sends a signal that this is technologically doable and this is something that maybe other systems are going to want to strive for,” he said.

articles.title_orig: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.title_zh: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.
Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”
“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”
The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.
The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.
Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”
The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.
The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.
“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K. , visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.title_zh: Bombardier Is Making a Big $270M Push in US
articles.content_orig:
Bombardier on Friday announced it is expanding in the United State investing $270 million, including $50 million in Wichita  as part of its commitment to growing the site’s capabilities and positioning it for future growth.
The Learning Center represents one component of Bombardier’s broader investment in Wichita. Inaugurated today, the new North American Learning Center reinforces the company’s commitment to developing talent, enhancing capabilities and supporting the long-term growth of its Kansas operations. A ceremony was held on site with Kansas Governor Laura Kelly, Lieutenant Governor David Toland, Bombardier senior leaders and industry stakeholders.
The Learning Center is Bombardier’s first dedicated in-house skills development center for newly hired aircraft technicians and mechanics from across America, helping build the skilled workforce needed to support the company’s growing service and support network, enhancing long-term care and convenience for customers. The program will foster continuous learning and provide employees with a strong foundation for their careers at Bombardier.
The approximately $50 million investment brings together investments in people, infrastructure and capabilities to strengthen the Wichita site for the future. In addition to the new Learning Center, the investment includes the recently expanded Wheel and Tire Shop, which combines state-of-the-art equipment with advanced employee training to expand Bombardier’s Component Repair and Overhaul (CR&O) capabilities, enhancing quality, efficiency and safety.
“Wichita has long been an important part of Bombardier’s story, and we continue to see tremendous opportunity for the site. Our approximately $50 million investment brings together important initiatives across the site, from the new Learning Center to expanded wheel and tire capabilities, strengthening both our people and our operations. This commitment to Wichita’s future will deepen the expertise and capabilities that will allow us to deliver an even stronger experience for our customers, while position the site for continued growth” said Paul Sislian, Executive Vice President, Aircraft Sales and Bombardier Aftermarket Services.
“Since 2019, my administration has partnered with Bombardier to build up the company’s presence in Wichita, which today now includes the new Learning Center, Bombardier Group’s U.S. headquarters, home of Bombardier Defense and the employment of 1,500 Kansans,” said Governor Laura Kelly. “Bombardier’s new $50 million investment underscores the enduring strength of the partnership between Bombardier and Kansas, and one that I expect will continue long into our shared future.”
With ten service and manufacturing facilities across America, including an upcoming service center in Fort Wayne, Indiana,(1) approximately 3,500 employees and a supplier spend of $2.5 billion across America, Bombardier continues to invest in the people, infrastructure and capabilities that support its customers. Wichita remains an important part of that footprint, with recent investments positioning the site to continue evolving alongside Bombardier’s services business and the needs of its customers.

articles.content_orig:
Dwindling academic programmes and official visits risk eroding the next generation of American China specialists
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.
Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.
However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure.

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Champi nears China after battering Taiwan, Japan
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.title_zh: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
articles.content_orig:
New research, facilitated by cutting-edge techniques, led to one of the first examples of physical proof for ancient ritual animal slaughter
Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival.
The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice.
To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial arrangement of valuable artefacts.

articles.title_orig: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.title_zh: Iran trying harder to target US personnel in Middle East, intelligence chief warns
articles.content_orig:
Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.title_zh: How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
articles.content_orig:
How Netanyahu reshaped Israel after 18 years in power
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.
Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.
As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.
Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.
Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.
The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.
In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.
Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.
Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law , which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.
Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.
Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.
A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.
Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.
Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.
Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests : a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.
In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.
But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.
At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.
Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.
But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

articles.title_orig: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.title_zh: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
articles.content_orig:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

articles.title_orig: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: US is reducing staffing at 4 Middle East embassies over increased threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.

articles.title_orig: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.title_zh: NASA Chief Warns China Is Closing Gap in ‘New Space Race’
articles.content_orig:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman warned Friday that the United States is in a "new space race" with China, saying that the agency must recapture the urgency of the Apollo era if it hopes to return astronauts to the moon first.
China launched its first astronaut in 2003, he said, and has since built up a broad portfolio of space capabilities, including lunar missions and plans for a crewed moon landing before 2030. These rapid advances have created a competition far closer than the Cold War race that culminated in the Apollo moon landings, Isaacman said, during an Artemis update at Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida.
"Nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass to our overseas competitors," he said. "The appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion."
NASA reaffirmed its summer plans for Artemis III, and for Artemis IV—the mission scheduled to return astronauts to the lunar surface—in 2028. The agency will continue to depend on Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to achieve these goals.
According to NASA officials, Artemis III will be a two-week mission involving four astronauts and a series of docking demonstrations in Earth's orbit, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing the lunar landers. The mission will not travel to the moon but is designed to test systems and operations needed for future lunar landings.
Artemis III will require multiple launches in quick succession from Florida and give crews an opportunity to conduct docking exercises with both commercial spacecraft, NASA leaders said.
During the briefing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons praised SpaceX's rapid development pace.
"We're seeing lots of hardware, lots of quick changes, and an absolute blistering pace of production," he said.
The agency's push comes as China works toward its publicly stated goal of landing astronauts on the moon before 2030, raising concerns among U.S. officials that America could lose momentum in a domain it once dominated.
Isaacman repeatedly invoked the Apollo era, arguing that NASA should draw lessons from when the agency progressed from Apollo 7's first crewed mission to Apollo 11's lunar landing within nine months.
"It's a playbook this agency knows really well, the same playbook that went from Apollo 7 splashdown to Apollo 11 in just nine months," he said.
While emphasizing that NASA will not compromise safety, Isaacman said the agency is working to cut bureaucracy, speed decision-making and increase the pace of hardware development.
The broader goal, he said, extends beyond simply returning astronauts to the moon.
"This will not be a repeat of flags and footprints," Isaacman said.
He described future lunar missions as laying the groundwork for a permanent human presence beyond Earth.
"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon, to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what will begin as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface, " Isaacman said.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here . Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins

articles.title_orig: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.title_zh: China’s AI compute power set to double, but heavily reliant on US chips: report
articles.content_orig:
China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year
China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research.
Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP).
While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.title_zh: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.
